The pause was only for a moment, •.uc. in that, short space of LI We el'ONtided with members eager to hear I..)enH speaking on his own side, .saw a strange a),,• subtle expression in the mask-like face. Ii seemed to grow set and rigid, the dark eyes were axed on the opposite wall as if the spea%er had t3uddenly seen something terrible, awc-inspiriir..;; the faint colour caused by the heat and the excitement of debate gave place to a death-like pallor; and the spectators almost held their breath as they looked at him.

But, whatever: the emotion. might have been, .it passed in an instant; the face again grew impassive, the clear, level voice flowed on in fluent, rhythmical sentences which carried con- _ __ltion with them.

The two old members, Mr. Welch and Mr. Bouchier, had exchanged glances, as the change had come over Talbot Denby's face, aid when the speech was over and the Government side of the House was cheering wildly, Mr. Bouebier whispered: • • • "What was the matter .with Denby just now ? "

Mr. Welch shook his head. "I dOn't know. A splendid speech. It will help them to carry the bill. But he looked bad just then, didn't he? I've not forgotten what you said about him some time ago; and to-night it seemed to me that you were right. That Man has something on Ids mind or conscience--"
"Say mind—conscience is out of date," said Mr. Bouchier.

"He is leading •.,a double life; and the other fife, the one that is not apparent to us, cropped up just then. If ever a man looked in mortal terror Denby did when he paused just now." There was, however; no terror on Talbot Denby's face as he left the House after receiving the thanks and approval of his whips, thanks all the more emphatic for their rarity—is there net more rejoicing on the Government benahes .over one repentant sinner than over a hundred righteous ?—and called a hansom. He told the man to drive to Rose. Cottage, Park-road, St. John's Wood, and he leant back in the cab and smoked a cigar with a serene and ylacid countenance, and with a smile of satisfac- tion hovering about his thin lips. He had scored heavily that night. All was going well with him. The cab pulled up at a pretty little house just peeping above a high- wall, the kind of house which, pretty though it May be, seems to shrink frbm its neighbours and crave for privacy. . .
_ A neat in-aid-servant let him in ; and_ as he went to the drawing-room, the door opened :Ind Fanny met him and threw her arms round his neck.

"Oh, how late you .are ! " she complained, but with smiles in her eyes and on her full, weak lips. "I seem to have been waiting days, months. Will yeti always be so late? It's so lonely, and I seem to have been away from home years,

years!" He soothed her and drew her to the sofa, "How fine you are already, my dear!" he said. She looked down at the ready-made dress she had bought—with the first money he had given her—and bridled with gratified vanity. "Do you like it? I'm so glad! I—l want to look like a lady, to he a lady, like what I ought to be. Yes, it is pretty, isn't it? It's a pity some of the folks at home can't see me. What would Susan Parks at the ,Cross Corners say, and that stuck up Goodwin at the Court, who thinks nobody's good enough for her, I Wonder ? "

He kissed her and clr.e'w her closer to him. "And you're quite happy, eh, Fanny? That's And you won't feel So lonely after a time. must take you about. You'll see London— London at last! And you'll forget the past." "The stupid old past! "she said, half-defiantly. "But it won't be easy. D'ye know I've had a letter from mother already." She giggled and nestled closer to him. "She says she hopes I like my situation. Situation! She little thinks I've got a couple of servants to wait on me ! " "They are not more than you deserve. You shall havelour if you like," he said, stroking her hair, but stifling a yawn—already! "You must write a nice long dutiful letter. We mustn't let her guess the truth, you know, Fanny. And what else does she say 9" "Oh, there's a lot of news," she replieil. "Miss Veronica's • still away; and the Earl doesn't seem well. Dr. Thorne has been up to the Court to see him. That's all, I think—oh! I'd nearly forgot. Mr. Groser, the -landlord of the Dog and Owl—you know the Dog and Owl, that low little public-house, you know ? " she explained with a contemptuous toss of her head. Talbot nodded. "I know. Well ? "

"He met mother yesterday and asked her .if she'd happened to ace a man as had been .staying at the Dog and Owl. A man called—l can't remember—oh, yes, Oatway—a man with a bandaged hand." Talbot's hand stopped in its caressing stroking of her hair, then went on again, but mechanically. ehe could not see his face, but it .had grown white, 'and his eyes 'wore the expression which they had done in the middle of his speech in the House.

!‘Well ? " he said, and his voice sounded so dry that Fanny moved ter hand so that she might look at his face ;' but he pressed her head closer to him and she 'sank down again with a little cooing murmur. "Groser, that's the landlord, told mother the man owed him some money for lodgings and some he'd lent him and had gone off suddenly, and he wanted to ;mow if mother or any of us had seen him. As if we should know anything about such a low person!" "As if indeed! murmured Talbot.

"But it's rather strange that I should know something," she continued, "for -I happened to see him the night before he disappeared, and it was the night • before—Ralph Farringdon went." She paused a moment before she spoke Ralph's name. "Oh!" said Talbot in a dry voice. •

„... Fanny nodded. "Yes. I happened to be at the cross road, and I saw Ralph Farringdon and this man Oatway. He'd stopped Ralph, or Ralph had stopped him, and they -were quarelling. I heard the man swear and Mr. Ralph speaking angrily, like as he was threatening, and Ithkught they were going to fight, so I ran home.” "Quite right," said Talbot. "Always run away when men are going to fight. Did you—did fou tell anyone of what you'd seen ? " Fanny. thought for *a moment. "Yes, I told mother, and I think I ,told Mr. Burehett—yes, I did; and I mentioned it to Goodwin when she came for the lace."

Talbot smiled grimly. "In fact, you told all the village," he remarked. She threw her head back and looked up at him, curiously. "What's the matter, lAtibot ?" she asked with surprise.- "You're quite white, and your voice is hoarse, as if you'd got a cold. Oh !' you aren't going to be ill? Let me get you something —it's brandy and some of that fizzy stuff you isn't it ?" . _ _ _

"Nothing is the .matter," he said, smiling. "I'm rather tired, that's all. l've been spenking in the Hou.se of Coirmons—oh, you wouldn't understand-- Thanks! But put your lips to it, first, Fanny; it will sweeten it
ciIArTEE, xxm.

Ralph reached Lontion "iin due course," as they say in commercial cireles, and put up for the night at a small hotel noar the station in the Waterloo-road. lie had had plenty of time for reflection during the iourney, and his reflections had brought him.sinall comfort. To be parted from the woman you love, with the prospect of meeting her again and nicking her your own, is had enough; but it is worse than bad when the chance of ever seeing her agaiN to say nothing of getting her for your wife, is so small as was Ralph' s. - He was well-nigh driven to despair -when he thought of Veronica—and when did he not think af her ?—but he refused to lose all hope, and the next morning he went down to the docks to seek I,ship for Australia. • He had very little. money and it was his inten- ;ion to work his passage out; but he was ;net with the difficulty which is, alas! not an incommon one in England. The supply of men just then exceeded the demand. He could not Ilford to remain idle while he waited for a ship, ;o the next morning he took his place amongst the dock labourers, and was soon engaged. it icemed to him, as he toiled at the bales and :cegs, that Lynne Court and all that had nappened there were but the baseless fabric of I.•dream. But the face and voice of Veronica ;tood out real enough in the vision, and all day he thought of her and of the. marvelksus, .ieredible fact that she loved him. _
His hotel was some way from the docks, but as his room cost but little he decided to remain

there Lntil he was fortunate enough to find a berth on one of the outgoing ships. The days passed in a grim and grey monotony, intensified by the terrible loneliness and solitude which oppress every man who lives in London with no friends. But presently he made at least one friend. In the room adjoining his at the hotel were a middle-acted woman and a little girl—a nurse and her charge, as Ralph rightly guessed. The child was a pretty little thing with all the charming ways of childhood, and once or twice Ralph had met her on the stairs and smiled at her, receiving a nod and a bright smile in return.
One evening, when he was going out to stroll about the crowded , streets in the hope of forgetting himself and his lost love, the woman

riusie out of the room with a basket on her arm, and stopped, with the door in her hand, to soothe the child who evidently did not like beinc, left. "I shan't be long, da," she said,,"ard now you be a good girl and play with your doll till nurse come S back; and perhaps nurse will bring you some sweeties."
She closed the door but stood listening, and Ralph heard a stifled little sob from within the room.
The woraam uttered a click of annoyance and distress.

"My little one don't like being left, sir," she said to Ralph, as if in explanation. "And I must go out and get some things." "It's natural," slid Ralph, sympathetically. "Solitude is not pleasant, and it's harder for children to bear than grown-up people. Is she an orphan?" "Oh, no, dear no!" replied the nurse,, still listening to the sounds of grief from within. "She's got a father, and he's coining by the next ship. Ada and me had to leave before him through an accident—and, oh, dear, I wish she wouldn't cry! I can't bear to leave her; and I can't take her with, me, because she's got a slight co!d ; and I wouldn't have her ill when her father comes for anything." "See here," said Ralph, "I've got nothing whatever to do, and was only going for an .hnless stroll; suppose I take your place while you're away? She and I Inv% met on the stairs now and again, and I'll try and keep her amused until you come back."_ _ _
The woman looked relievefl, but a little doubtful.

"Oh, I couldn't think of troubling you, sir," she sal; "not that she's a troublesome child, and she have took quite a fancy to you—the Big Man, she calls you—but--" "Oh, that's all right," said Ralph. "I'm fond of children; you can leave her in my charge safely enough. You won't be gone long, I daresay." The nurse hesitated for a moment only•as she glanced at the hand Some, bronzed face, then nodded gratefully, and, opening the door, said: ."Ada, here is sotheone- who will keep you company." "I don't want no comrany," sobbed Ada, but she came to the door, and when she saw Ralph her pretty little face brightened. "Oh, it's the Big Man !" she said, with sudden cheerfulness. .

"Come along, little woman, let's keep each other company," said Ralph, with his infectious smile; and before the nurse had left them the child was sitting on Ralph's knee, and completely engrossed in a wonderful .-rabbit, which, com- posed only of his •handkerchief, actually pricked up its ears, cleaned itself with its paws, and nibbled at her frock. It was not only a wonder- ful rabbit, but it had apparently a most romantic history, which Ralph told in a manner so capti- vating that Ada leant her head against hi S breast and gazed up at him with all her hale soul enthralled.
When the nurse returned silo fOund Ralph seated on the stairs with the child asleep in .his arms.
"She's just gone off," he whispered, stopping her profuse thanks. "I'll carry her in, if you'll let me; it's a pity to wake her."
He carried -her into the room and laid her down in the cot, and the nurse followed him out to express her gratitude.

"I'm sure it's very .kind of you, sir," she said. "And I'm sure her father will thank you when he arrives. It's wonderful how she's took to you, for Miss Ada is rather particular in her. likes and dislikes."

Ralph smiled at the dubious compliment, and, lighting his pipe, went out with a lighter heart than he h Id owned since he had left Lynne. The next day when he returned from work the child was waiting for him at the top of the stairs, and leaped into his arms with that abandon which is simply irresistible to a man with Ralph's tenderness of heart. "'Ave you dot the rabbit, Big Man ? " she asked wistfully, as she clung round his neck. _ _ _ _ _ _

The nurse -Came out aiid scolded her for worrying the gentleman, but Ralph begged that she Might come into his room while he had his ..ea, at whie'i not only a rabbit but a barn-door fowl put in an appearance. From that day the child and he were fast friends; and he looked forward to seeing her elfish form on the .stairs waiting for him, and still more for the loving embrace with which she welcomed him. Gradually., as the nurse's confidence increased,the two became so necessary to each other that Ralph often in the evening took Ada for a walk. They would saunter along, the child clinging to his hand, through the big thoroughfares, Ralph, with his pipe in his mouth, pointing out the objects likely to be of interest td a child, and answering her innumer- able questions. How great a comfort'. and con- solation her love and companionship were to the broken-hearted man no pen could set down; it is possible they saved him from utter despair. One day he succeeded in finding a vessel that would take him, and he was trying to tweak the news of their approaching parting to Ada, when she startled him by saying: "MY papa's coming, to-morrow. I'm so glad; aren't 'oo ? I 'ope oo'll be as fond of him as 'oo are of me, Big Man. 'Oo are fond of me, aren't 'oo.? " • ..

"Very," said Ralph. "And so papa is coming! I'm very glad for your sake; though I'm afraid we shan't see so much of each other. Look at the soldiers, Ado! They're going clown to the Bank to tatke care of all the money there." "Is all the money dere ? " she asked, after she nad stared at the guard marching past them. "P'raps that's where papa's money is • he said ke'd lost nearly all of it. Do 'oo think he'll find it dere ?"

"I hope so," said Ralph. "And now I think we'll have to turn back. We'll just get a packet of that special chocolate of yours, eh, Ada, and then we'll toddle home." His heart ached not a little that night, for he knew that he should lose his little companion; and, sure enough, next evening there was no Ada to welcome him on the stairs. He heard a 'man's voice mingling with hers in the room next his, and knew that her father had arrived. Although he himself was to start in three days' time, he felt as if he had been bereaved, and thought, as he knocked out his pipe and prepared for bed, that he was doomed to lose everything he loved.

Veronica also reached London "in due course " ; and she also had had plenty of time for reflection during the journey. In the enthusiasm of her love for Ralph she had fled from the ,Court with the intention of following him; but, long before the train had reached the terminus, she realised that it was easier to resolve than to accomplish. In the first place, she was not sure that Ralph would go to Australia, or that he would go at once; and, .mpposing he had gone, she did net know which part he would ship for. But her earlier know- ledge and experience of London stood her in good stead, and she was not daunted by the diflleulr-s in her way. It seemed to her that the best thing she could do would be to go back to her old .rooms in Camden Town where she was known; and she was getting into -a cab, when a voice spoke her name. She looked round and 'its‘r a young girl who had been a fellow-lodger of hers. At sight of her, Veronica's heavy heart leaped. And yet she had almost forgotten the girl's name! But in that moment of lonelifless, in the midst of the great crowd, it came back to her as, readily as if, days instead of years had passed since she and Martha Ludlow had dwelt together in the grimy lodging- house in Camden Town. "Martha!" she cried, holding out her hand. "Is it really you _
The girl ;hook friendly. surprise.
hands and eyed her with

now, to think of meeting you, Miss Denby! Why, I thought you'd' gone away to live with some swells, and that I shouldn't set eyes on yen again." "But y-.lu hate, you see," said Veronica, as cheerfully as she could. "I have VAMP to IiVO in

London again. 1 am going back to the old place; will you come with me? Jump in.,, Martha laughed—the Cockney laugh of pleasant . "Why, what's the use of going there?" she said. 'lt's pulled down and turned into a shop; the whole row is, long ago." Veronica leoked dismayed. "Oh, then, don't know where to go!" she said almost to herself. • Martha's sharp eye scanned her narrowly.- "If 1 you ain't too particular, you might come with me," she said. 'l'm living in Sowerhy-street it's near here, and there's a vacant room—s couple of 'em, if they're good enough. Anyhow, you'll have to make up your mind pretty quicl. if you don't want the cabman to have a fit. Veronica nodded in her quick way. "I'll come. Jump, in," she said. , In less than ten minutes they had reached the house. It was in a poor but decent street, and the two girls struck a bargain with the landlady, and Veronica, almost ~breathless with the. speed with which circumstance had taken her in hand, found herself tenant o" t\-0 rooms in No. 6, bowerby-street, S. W. As the girls sat ore- tea in Martha's - room, it was Martha who talked ; and she related her uneventful life, since she had last seen Veronica, in a quick and hurried manner, as if she did not want Veronica to think there was any necessity for confidences on her part. But while Martha Was explaining that she was working at a.factory close by, Veronica had beer. considering how much she could tell of her past life, and at last said, with a touch of colour in her face: "And now I ought to tell you all that has hapeened to me. But I can't, Martha!" -I.'m surel don't want you to, Miss Denby," :Thoth,. put in. "I always knew you was a lady, one of the swells, and I. thought you'd gone to live with rich, and high-born people, like you read of in the novelettes, you know. Thinking of you goin..; away like you did ! .I've often thought that after all there may be some, truth in them!" "Yes, I have been living with rich people," said Veronica; "but I have left them, and am- , quite poor again. See, that's. all the money I have. 4. She displhyed her purse, but without producing the effect she, with her recent acquaintance with wealth, had expected. "Loa, why it's a fortune.! .And I Was going to ask you if you'd care to go to the factetty with me! " exclaimed Martha. "But, goodness, ,you're a reglar Creeses!" "But I don'st ' want to spend this," said Veronica. ""-And I shall he very glad if you can get sonic work for me to do at home. Do you think you can ? You know that lam tolerably quick with my needle." Martha said that she thought she could, and Veronica drew a breath of satisfaction. It seemed to her that she would find some relief for her aching heart in hard work, and some conso- lation in the fact that she, as well as Ralph. was living a life' of toil. The girls talked far into the night, and at last Veronica went_ to bed _ _

„ —to dream that she and Ralph were married and were working hard for their living ; but, ah, so happy, with a happiness which turned this commonplace earth to paradise! The next day she inquired her way to the shipping-agents at the docks, and made inquiries respecting the vessels that were starting for Australia. One had sailed that morning, and the clerk, fascinated by the beautiful face and sweet voice, shewed her the passenger list. But the name. of Ralph Farringdon was not in it, anithe clerk, with some surprise at her question, told her that it would be impossible to discover the names of the hands. "And most of 'em ship under false names, too, miss.”

Veronica returned to Sowerby-street with the feeling of helpless despair which must have been experienced by the individual who first engaged in the historic task of hunting for a needle in a bottle of hay: but Martha that night brought home some work for her to do; and Veronica almost dew at it as a source of relief from her anxious thought and Ilonging. If she had only had the courage to dery the Earl and keep Ralph at .Lynne, or better—oh, still far better l—insisted upon going with him !. But the Earl had hypnotised them both with his worldly wisdom and cynical heartlessness, and she and Ralph were divided! Almost daily she went down to the shipping office and the clerk, now quite head .over ears in love with her, did all he could to help her. But there was no trace of Ralph. And yet, if she had but thought of seeking amongst the labourers at the docks, she would have found him; indeed, once she passed within a few yards 0',7 the spot where he was toiling. She grew thinner and paler as the days went on; for, when she went Out for the walk'which Martha, who was anxious about her, insisted

on, all her thoughts were of Ralph, and she was always seeking him, with all her mind and soul absorbed in the search. Absence makes the heart grow fonder, when that heart really loves. and Veronica knew now how dearly she loved him, how necessary he was to her happiness. She felt like one dragging wearily through a desert where no water is. For love is the water of life, and to thirst for it is to know fully what anguish is. , One aftetnoon she was walking home from her quest, when a gentleman passed her, paused, then, after a moment's consideration, turned, and, following here lifted his bat. "Miss Denby ? " he said, hesitatingly, as if in doubt. •

Veronica started, and turned quickly and nervously. She saw an elderly man with a weather-beaten face and grey hair. He was dressed in a rough serge su;t somewhat the worse foe wear.; but both faLe and figure were that of a gentleman. "It is Miss Denby, is it not ? "le said, with a smile. "I'm 'afraid you don't remember •me. My name is Saintsbur). We met at a dinner-party at my cousin's—the Hall is near Lynne. Court, you knovi."

Veronica's brows unbent. "Oh, of course, yes!" she said. "1 rememb3r you. You are Mr. George Saintsbury." • He smiled rather grimly. "Yes, the black sheep of the family, you know." • Veronica cOldured and shook hands with him. "Are you staying in -town ?" he asked rather hesitatingly, for he had noticed the plainness of her dress and the pallor of her face. "Yes, I am living in London, Mr. SaintSbury," said Veronica. "I have left •Lynne Court. Oh! and I ought to ask you, please, not to tell them ,at the Hall that you have seen me. I—l—it is too long a story, but I am estranged from Lord Lvnborough and have left the Court—for ever! " He inclined his head. "I am sorry," he said, with the quiet sympathy of the gentleman. "I hope you are'—you are eared for here in Loudon, and : r not alone—not without friends ? " "No," said Veronica, as quietly. "I. am living with an old friend, a girl I knov,-. I have quite cut myself off froth the old life, and that is why I asked--" "You have nothing to fear from your Meeting with me, Miss Denby," he said, gravely. "In no ease should I tell anyone that I have. met you, as you do not wish me to do so ; but, indeed, I am not likely to have an opportunity of telling my people. I, too. am estranged .from them. I have had a run of had luck— my own fault, my own fault !—and I have just retnrnad from Australia where I have failed in an undertaking. But I need not bore you with that." "Australia!" said Veronica. For your true lover everything turns on one pivot. Perhaps could help her to find Ralph. "Yes," be said, noting her sudden eagerness. "Is there anything I can do for you ? Are yon . interested in Australia ? I am staying at an hotel near here—quite a modest little place—with my child, my Ada. 1 should like you to see her. She is the sWeetest-7-Ilit I must not indulge in a father's rhapsodies, though, of course, I am very proud of her. She is all the world to me. Will you come and see her? She has no lady friend, no ene but her old nurse. But it is asking too much, Miss Denby!" "I will conic with you and see her," said Veronica. • She turned and walked With him, and he talked of his bad luck, of his people at the Hall, but mostly of the child. As they talked a fire-engine dashed past them. They reached the street in which the hotel stood, and to their surprise they found themselves in the midst of a huge crowd fringed round a couple of fire-engines at work. The .street was full of smoke, and flames were springing from one of. the houses. George Saintsbury uttered a cry of terror that thrilled Veronica. "The hotel !" he gasped. "It is the hotel! Ada!" He forced. his way through the shouting mob, .and Veronica her heart beating painfully, mechanically followed him. It was the hotel, and it was burning fiercely. In a LITOUD in the centre eleared lw the fireman

were the landlord and the people belonging fa the place, and they were gazing with horror- stricken eyes at the windows through which the smoke and flames were issuing. As Mr. Saints- bury rushed towards them crying hoarsely "My child! Ada! Ada! Have you got my child ? " a woman—the nurse—threw herself upon him, and, elutching him, cried iik tones of agony: "She's in there. in Oh. Heavens. master, save her! I'd gone out—l left her for a finv minutes. She's nut here—all the rest are saved. Oh, the child, the child!"
The distracted father would have rushed to the burning house, but a stalwart fireman caught Him and held him back though he struggled_ 11,reely.

Vero-nica stood, wringing her hands and almost fainting under the strain of the terrible scene but she was roused to full consciousness by a roar that went up from the spectators. A young man bad made his way through the crowd, had paused a moment to: look at thi house, as a General might pause to scan a fortress he intended to assail, then had plunged into the doorway.

IF had come and disappeared so cuickly that the firemen had been una'Ae to stop him, and the crowd roared still more excitedly when, a, moment or two later, he .7cs seen at one of the. upper windows with a child in his arms. Be was framed by the blackened win,4ow, through which the smoke belched ;11 a thick volume, and the flames darting from one below lit up his face. Veroniea, gazing with horror, uttered a cry and staggered, for to her ove,- wroughtmind it seemed to be the face of Ralf h!

He-held the child .to his breast and looked down as if waiting, looked down with an apparent calmness and assurance which was not misplaced, for the firemen shouted encouragingly. The fire- escape had not arrived—alas !here in England wes are not abreast of the times in the matter of our fro department, and our gallant firemen are ortvn sadly handicapped by the lack of proper appliances—but some of the men stretched out a tarpaulin beneath the window, and the man who held the child saw it, and, stooping as low as possible, gently dropped his still living burden. A roar of applause went up from ill crowd as the;itther rushed forward and caught her to his breast. But the roar grew more frantic, almost savage in its intensity, as the rescuer was seen to stagger and fail against the now burning window-frame as if he were swooning. _
"Jura-p, jump, for Heaven's sake!" yelled the crowd.

Veronica's tongue cave to the roof of her mouth, and she could not cry out, but her beftrt-, seemed bursting as her strained eyes were fixed on the -figure amidst the flames and smoke. "Jump! Jump ! " cried the crowd again, and. the roar, almost drowning the crackling of the burning woodwork and the fall of the walls, seemed to reach the ears of the man. He was seen to pass his hand over his face as if he were struggling for breath, then he mounted to the window sill and dropped. A shout of satisfaction, a moan of doubt, arose from the thousands of throats as the crowd saw him fall. He was caught in the tarpaulin, and some of the firemen closed round him while others kept back the-frantic and half-maddened mob. Borne forward by the press, Veronica found herself amongst those surrounding him. The flames lit up the scene and fell upon his face., A ell rose from her parched lips, a cry that went to the heart of the firemen, accustomed as they were to such scenes.
"Ralph! Ralph t" , The name pierced the air, and, as she uttered it in the accents of a woman's anguish and terror, she fell on her knees beside him. f , • (To be continued.)

div.p: THE VERDICT OF THE ITEL-k RT.
13y CHARLES GARVICE,
Aathor of "Her Heart's Desire," "In Cupid's Chains," "Just a Girl," "Nance," "The Out- cast of the Family'," "A Corouet of Shame," 45:4:6

div.head: CHAPTER, XXII.
div.p: CHAPTER, XXII.

Lr'anny Mason heard of Ralph's departure when ehe went down to the hut the neat morning to "tidy up,” "Gone ! " she cried, almost dropping her broom and staring at Durchett with pale, aghast face. "I —I saw him last night with a bundle on his back, but I thought he was going to tile town; 'I didn't think--" She turned her head away to hide her face. "Why, whatever made him go, and so sudden, Mr. Burchett ?" "That's his business, not mine, nor yours," he peplied, grimly. "When the last woman's dead, curiosity will be buried with her. You're late this morning." , - • -

"-I overslept myself, and mother was busy," said Fanny, sullenly. She was suffering badly, but from wounded pride rather than love; for it is not given to her kind to love deeply. "If I'd known ho was going I'd have spoken to him, and perhaps " She tossed her head and bit her lip„ . • _ . .

"NOthing you could have said would have kept him back. He went on important business," said Burchett. He Was leaving the hut when Mr. Talbot Denby came through the clearing. He looked particularly well; the pallor and haggard expres- sion had left his face, and there was a touch of colour in his .sallow cheeks, and his eyes were bright. Everything had gone Well with him, and he was to hear yet further good news. 'sl2kood-morning, Burchett," he, said. "I just .00kedlin to ask you how the birds were doing. I rather think we may have a shooting party this season."

"Things are looking very well, sir," replied Burchett. "A shooting party? I shall have, to get an extra hand or two; and I've just lost a good one. I'arringdon's gone." Talbot did not start, but his face became like a mask.

"Indeed!" he said. "Dissatisfied, I suppose ? Well, I should think he was a good riddance. Where has he gone? Another situation ? " "No., sir. I think he's making for Australia, where he came from." ,

• Talbot's heart leaped with relief and satis- faction. Certainly his lucky star was in the ascendant, and Fate seemed to be removing with one sweep of the hand every Obstacle in his path. Burchett was passing on, but paused. "Perhaps you'd be kind enough to tell Miss Veronica that I'll send up the roots of the wall- flowers she asked me for, sir," he said. "I can Move 'em now."
Veronica had some time ago admired some gentian and wild orchids which she WO seen near the hut.

Talbot nodded. "You need not trouble. Miss Veronica has left the Court," he said, casually. "She has gone to pay some visits, and will be away some time." • Burchett touched his cap and walked away, -.ad Talbot was following, when Fanny, who had been listening, caine to the door. She looked very pretty, with the sunlight falling on her face and golden hair; her cheeks were flushed with the emotion which had been evoked by the tidings of Ralph's departure, and Talbot in this moment of, his elation was in the humour to admire her. Usually he was quite unimpressionable. "Good-morning," he said, ingratiatingly. are Fanny Mason, are you net " "Yes, sir," assented Fanny, dropping a curtsey and blushing with pleasure at the notice of the great Mr. Talbot. "Ah, yes, I remember. Of course! I remember you when you were quite a little girl; you were pretty even then. You and I used to play together when we were small children. I haven't seen very much of you lately, but that is because lam so seldom at the Court. How hot it is! I think [will come in and rest for a little while."
"You

He went into the hut and sat down, and continued to talk to her as she Worked. The relief from the awful strain was so great that he felt delighted with himself, with this :girl, with the very air he breathed. Presently he asked for some water; but Fanny brought him a glass of milk, and, as he took it from her hand, he looked up at her with a smile that set poor weak Fanny's heart all in a flutter. And the heart, sore with Ralph's desertion, was, so to olak, on the rebound; it was not difficult for Talbot Denby to catch it. "You're too pretty and—and clever a girl to waste your sweetness on the desert air of Lynne, Fanny," he said. "You ought to be in London. You would see something of life then; you are buried alive down here amonvt a set of yokels and chawbacons. You've nevem been to London, I suppose ? " At the moment he liai no definite object in view, and the desire to flirt with the girl was born of his mood, of his sudden exaltation ; but Fanny's downcast looks and blushes flattered him.

"Oh, no, no!" she said, timidly. "But I've heard of it; and, oh! how I should like to go." "Well, we must see about it," he said. "I will try and find a place for you. I think I know a lady who would take you." Fanny blushed still morn .eeply; and ll'ar weak, pretty face was alighz with the plea,surable emotions that chased over it.

"Oh, if you would, sir !" she breathed. "I'm so tired of this place! It iPlet life as you say, sir." "And you ought to see iite he 'put in, smoothly. Really, with her complexion of milk- and-roses and her foolish, child-like eyes she was. very taking. "I'll see what I can do. But I think I wouldn't say anything about it, Fanny, in case it came to nothing. I daresay we shall meet again. Let me see, you live in the cottage on the hill? There's a lane behinil it, I remember. Now, suppose you meet mu some evening; shall we say to-morrow, after dinner?" Fanny nodded eagerly. To meet the great Mr. Talbot of the Court, and secretly! The honour of it nearly turned her weak little brain. . "Oh, I'm so grateful ; it's so kind of you, sill!" she murmured, with suppressed excite- ment. "I cant thank you, sir!"

"Oh; yes, you can !" he said with a smile. "There are better ways gf expressing 9ne's thanks than by words, Penny. Don't you know one of them ? Let me teach you." He put his arm round her, and, raising her ace, looked down at her with a smile, :and kissed Mr.

! "Oh, I forgot.!" he said, in a low voice. "It was you who should have done that, wasn't it ? " ; She hung her head for a moment, then. she raised it slowly and kissed him. i -Mr. Talbot left the hut with the smile still on his face. The little flirtation with Fanny had made his heart still lighter. After all, there were other ways of amusing oneself than at the gaming-table. And she really was very pretty and tempting; not an icicle of a woman, like ,y4ronica, for instance. For a moment or two he himself where she had gone—had her msibppearance anything to do with Ralph Farringdon's ? The gnostic* drove the smile from his face and drew his dark brows together; but he thrust it from him. It was .sufficient for • him that she had gone and left the field clear for , him.

As for Fanny, Mr. Talbot's "kindness" had soothed the wound inflicted on her vanity by Ralph's. departure. She could almost thinft of ' him contemptuously—for what was a gamekeeper compared to Mr. Talbot of the Court! And Mr. Talbot had kissed her, whereas Ralph had actually refused her proffered lips. She met Mr. Talbot in the lane the next evening, and for several following evenings; for. • he lingered at the Court, though the whips of his party sent him the usual imperative notices from the House of Commons."

A week later Fanny shewed her mother a letter she had received from a lady in London, a lady in St. John's Wood, who required a servant. Mrs. Mason was opposed to Fanny's accepting the offer, but Fanny overrode her mother's opposition, and one morning she started for her "situation."

Mr. Talbot Denby had left the Court the preceding night. v One evening a little later he was in his place at the House, and spoke in support of a bill introduced by his party. stoke with more than hi,

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

:MEETING OF THE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE. The Parochial Committee met on Tuesday evening at the Hall Restaurant, Stockton Heath. Mr. George Tiling presided, and there were also present : Messrs. J. H. Clarke, J. Mynekyme, H. 3. Westbrook, T. West- brook, F. Pearson, J. W. Bouchier, J. Hallows, G. J. Brown, J. McDermid, F. Warburton. J. swinton (turveyor), and George F. Ashton (clerk to tßle Rural 'District Council). POSTAL FACILITIES. The Clerk read the following letter be had received from the Postmaster of Warrington :—" Dear sir,—l beg to inform you that a collection of letters from the Walton-road box, on Sundays, at 7.30 p.m., will be made in future, commencing next Sunday, the Bth inst. With respect to keeping open the Stockton Heath sub-office on week-dflys until the last collection this ispot practic- able' but an effort is being made to get 'one of the .ahopkeepers'.jn the vicinity of the office to sell stamps, under licence, until 9.30 p.m. The question of additional deliveries in Stockton Heath is now under consideration. It was decided to thank the Postmaster for his consideration. THE SEWAGE SYPHoN_UNDER THE SHIP

CANAL. The Clerk said he bad received the following letter from Mr. W. Henry Hunter, Chief Engineer to the Ship Canal Company, with reference to a resolution complaining of the state of the sewage syphon under the Ship Canal, or Twenty-steps Bridge.—" I have epqnired into the matter. The syphon in question has how been working since the opening of the Canal, and there has heen no complaint raised in regard to it. Recently the sewage from Walton, Sc., conveyed by the hew sewer along Ellesmere-road has been turned into the syphon, and, therefore, the conclusion is irresistible that the alleged nuisance is due to the new works recently carried out. Under these circumstances I. cannot see that it is the duty of the Ship Canal Com- Pliny to make good the defects in the sewering of Walton and Stockton Heath." The Clerk said he had replied to the letter to the faPct that he would fully investigate the point which nad been raised, but he felt sine the nuisance com- plained of was in existence long before any sewage from Walton was turned into the syphon' (Hear, bear.) _ _ . .
Air: H. J. Westbrook: The. fact that we have. not complained before shows that we are a long-suffering race, and that we should call upon the company to carry out what we ask for. _ _

Mr. Brown said he had received wholesale corn- Plaints about the matter, and it was a wonder they had not had fever. Something should be done either by the Ship Canal Co. or by someone else. (Hear, hear.) It was decided to ask a representative of the Company to meet the Clerk and the Surveyor to discuss the reatte.r.

div.head: DRESS-FASMION-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASMION-HOME.
THE SQUARE-CET BODICE.

Evening dress this autumn will be character- ii ised by the re " rn of the square-cut bodice. This very becomin fashion usually results in the bodice being ther higher; an effect which Can be borne without distress when one remembers the evening fr gowns of litst season. It is becom- ing to the figure and becoming to the face. At the back it ,may be modified with a "V," but for full evening wear it is square both back and front. We shall also sue our old friend the shoulder-strap, supporting a bodice Whose upper line is continued unbroken across the arms, leaving the, top of .the arm visible between sleeve anti strap. ' This is a pretty way of setting off one of the beauties shared by most people; the top of the arm is a most graceful cave. -So long as the shoulder-strap remains fairly substantial, there is nothing to object to, remarks the Globe; but before it last vanished from among us it had dwindled to, the size and apparently much less than the strength of a bootlace.

div.head: SMART AUTT7MN COAT.
div.p: A SMART AUTT7MN COAT.

Though coats of half-a-dozen shapes and lengths will be worn during the autumn and coming winter, the simple, three-quarter offair, slightly cut away in front, will undoubtedly be one of the most fashionable. models. Just such a coat is pictured in our sketch, the material in which it is realised being a fine satin-faced black cloth of good quality and medium weight. The Coat fastens in single-breasted fashion with half-a-dozen large and handsome black buttons, both fronts, as well as the bottom of the coat,

being finished with a line of machining near the edge. From the neck turns back a smart little roll collar, the upper part of which is carried out in black velvet, the under, in white cloth braided with black soutache. The coat itself is cut to fit with a certain amount of ease, but to give all the appearance of being a tight-fitting model, the basques being rounded in front and fairly full over the hips. Cuffs of black velvet and braided white cloth finish the , simple full- length sleeves and repeat the idea of the collar.

div.head: USE FOR CARDBOARD BOXES.
div.p: A USE FOR CARDBOARD BOXES.

A good effect may be arrived at, says a Queen corre<Pondent, by taking a cardboard box to pieces and covering the sections with some material by lacing it tightly over with cotton, then cutting coarse brown paper exactly to the same ,size as the cardboard, covering them with some plain material, and joining them together; then put the joined sections to- gether, pierce them near the upper and lower edges, pass ribbon through, and tie tightly together. The lid is arranged in the same way. Thus the pretty covered box can be untied for travelling and Afterwards quickly readjusted. The bottom .of the box should be sewn to the four sides before the ribbon ties are threaded through the holes. Waste-paper baskets can also be arranged in the same way, using cast- aside cardboard boxes. Cut a base with four or six sides, then cut the upright pieces to corre- spond, sew them to the base, and join the sides with ribbon ties. The sewing is quite simple, as the needle passes through the material and not the cardboard. Cardboard boxes that are sent from shops with new gloves can be covered in the way I have described, and con- verted into very ornamental ones. If a plain linen or silk is used, a name, monogram, or floral spray should be worked on the top. Inex- pensive and most acceptable presents can thus be made with very little trouble. A CHIC AUTUMN HAT.

There is a pronounced vogue among smart milliners this autumn for an alliance of brown with grey, the favourite shades being a warm and beautiful golden-brown combined with a delicate silvery grey. The charming hat of our sketch forms an excellent illustration of this pretty mode, and is very typical of up-to-date autumn millinery. The hat itself, of lovely

golden-brown velvet, is of the favourite cloche shape, and has a rather high crown and wide curving brim, the latter, by the way, being lined with satin of exactly the same shade as the velvet. In front of the chapeau, coming, well down on to the brim, and completely hiding the crown, is perched a ,huge bird, of shape and plumage utterly unknown to the natural world. The head is slightly suggestive of the seagull both in colour and form, but it is provided with delicate fluffy feathers of an enchanting grey, flecked faintly here and there with streaks of golden brown. The back of the hat is finished with a smart bow of brown satin, the tail feathers of the bird coming so far round as almost to conceal it.

div.head: AUTUMN MATERIALS.
div.p: AUTUMN MATERIALS.

Amongst the new materials displayed for wear this autumn, nothing ie more popular, says Lon- don Opinion, than the soft faced cloths with shaded stripes which promise to become the rage before long. Coats and skirts, frocks and cloaks, alike are being made of the new material. Tar- tans—as usual at this time of the year—have made their appearance, while striped velvet is being made up for more ,matronly modes. Long coats promise to hold their own in the new styles, and the latest skirt is fashioned with no fulness at the top, but spreading to an enormous width at the hem

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

BOILED PARTRIDGE AND CABBAGE. Cut two white-heart cabbages into quarters, wash them well, and blanch in salted water for ten minutes. Then strain, press until dry, and remove the hardest part. Take old partridges, truss them as for boilang, line the bottom of a stewpan with a few slices of bacon, carrots, turnips, and onions cut in slicer, place the birds on the top, surround with the pieces of cabbage, and cover with a bouquet of herbs, a few peppercorns, salt, lb. of sausages, and a fair-sized piece of fresh butter. Cover with stork ra nr4 gtow for three-auarters of an noun Then remove the partndges, ana con- tinuo cooking the cabbages for another forty- five minutes.. Strain off the liquor, heat up the birds again in it, and serve surrounded by the cabbage and sausages split in halves. Pear the taut* round and serge.

div.head: Examiner., Saturday, September 28, 1907.
div.p: The Examiner., Saturday, September 28, 1907.
OUR LOCAL GIURCIES.
Workingmen.s Mission. sank Quay.

The Chapel Anniversary Service' in connection with this Place were held on Sunday. Councillor James Ball was the preacher in the morning, and Mr. Goslin, of Earlestown, occupied the pulpit in the evening. In the afternoon a musical service was held. Mr. E. W. Jones presided and delivered a short but earnest address. Solos were ably rendered by Miss Davies, of liollinfare, and Mr. E. Pearce of Warrington. The anthems by the choir were plenainglv. given. Mr. Atkinson manipulated the organ, and Mr. Millington acted as conductor. The collections for the day amounted to £5 IGs. St. Barnabas' Church.

! The Ifarvest thanksgiving services were continoed on Sunday and were largely attended. At the choral cele- bration of the Holy Communion in the morning the preacher was the Rev. H. B. Firth, Vicar of St. James', Latchford, who drew some useful lessons from the analogy between the growth of the corn and the development of human character. A children's service in the afternoon was addressed by the Rev. G. R. Oakley, Vicar of Dea,rnley, Rochdale, who also occupied the pulpit at Evensong, and spoke up-m the harvest as an evidence of the Resurrection. Tner,a was a very large congregation, the church being filled. The choir acquitted themselves most creditably, the music being l of an appropriately joyous character and including the anthem Bless the Lord." The Nfognificat and Nunc Dimittis were sung to special settings. Mr. T. Evans presided at the organ.

div.head: Padgrale Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Padgrale Wesleyan Church.

There were large congregations at the Wesleyan Church, Padgate. ou Sunday, when harvest thanksgiving services were held. As usual the chnrch had been very prettily decorated by a willing band of lady workers, the pulpit and communion table being especially effective. The morning preacher was the newly- appointed minister to the Warrington circuit, the Rev. Thomas Miller, while the pulpit was occupied in the evening by the Rev. Sidney Pitt, superintendent of the circuit. The Rev. Thomas Miller c mincted a young people's service in the afternoon. The services were most successful throughout, the choir acquitting them- selves very creditably, rendering the anthems " Fear not, 0 land "and "Toe earth is the Lord's," in excel- lent style. Mr. Hugh' Mellor presided at the organ. The offertories which were on behalf of the church funds, showed an advance of 21. 4s. over last year.
Rev. Sidney Pitt and Methodiat Re-union.

The Rev. Sydney Pitt conducted the service at Bewsey-road Wcsleyan Church on Sunday morning. In giving out the hymn "The Church's one foundation" be referred to the United Methodist Conference which had been held during the previous week at City-road Chapel, London. Be expressed the thankfulness of the congregation that the divisive elements operating on Methodism some fifty or sixty years ago seemed now to have spent, their force and that a new spirit was beginning to prevail. The three minor Methodist bodies had united, the Primitive Methodists and the Mother Church still being prevented from coming into organic union. He hoped and prayed, however, that the day might speedilyv come when there might be a united Methodism in Great Britain, as there already was in several colonies, and he trusted that no consideration of pride or self-will on either side would be allowed to prevent so desirable a consumrna- tion.—The organist (Mr. W. Pearce) played the Dead March in" Saul" in memory of the late 3Ir.W. Looker, a highly respected member of the congregation who recently passed away. THE REV. W. MELLOR'S VIEWS.

The subject of Methodist Union was also referred to at Bold-street Church on Sunday evening by the Rev, W. Mellor. After giving a brief account of the three denominations concerned, the preacher said they must all rejoice in the union which had Nen effected, for it would strengthen the influence of Methodism in this country, which had always been a beneficent influence. And more than that it brought within measurable distance the union of all the Methodist bodies and the formation of one English Methodist Church, a union which he believed some of them wonld live to see. He could not help .asking " What is there to prevent it ?" There were no doctrinal differences whatever, and as for the differences in Church polity those could bq overcome, and would be overcome if they realized how small they were—smaller now than ever, and being small they should not be allowed to stand in the way. Re-union would do away with the overlapping—the competition he was about to say which existed in so many places, involving a waste—a sinful waste, he ventured to say, of time, money, energy, and influence. It would pro- mote spiritual efficiency, arid instead of their devoting themselves so much to the raising of money to support weak and unnecessary comes, they would .he able to devote themselves more tb real spiritual work It wonid also take an argument out of the moutbs of unfriendly critics, yet critics not devoid of good sense, who asked, "How is it that you Methodists, holding the same doctrines, and in the main naving the same kind of church organization, cannot agree to worship together, and work together, and be one ? " Best of all, such a union would be a carrying out of the spirit of the peti- tion of the text, "that they all may bo one." He could not think for a moment that it was in accordance with the mind and purpose of the Master that there should be so many varieties of churches, giving rise to so much variance. So many sects, involving—though perhaps not necessarily—so much sectarianism. Unity, he knew, did not mean uniformity, and perhaps it would be too much to say that they were to look forward to the time when the Church on earth would be one vast visible organization, holding the same view on all points, and conforming to one 'ecclesiastical order of things ; but he (lake thought that they might hope for for the day when " Our unhappy divisions" would be much fewer, add receive less emphasis.

div.head: Bishop Eldridge at Emmanuel Church.
div.p: Bishop Eldridge at Emmanuel Church.

Three very interesting services were held on Sunday at the shove Church, the Right Rev. Bishop Eldridge, D.D..heing the prescher.The occasion was the env rersary of the opening of the Institute,Einutsford-road and the visit of the Bishop was also made use of for admitting to the lay ministry two young men of the congregation and eighteen candidates were presented and confirmed at the evening service. Before giving out his text ,in the morning Dr. Eidridge referred to the work of the Institute which, he said, had already proved most important in connection with the service of God and bad received the manifest favour of,liim. He trusted that the future would be full of gladness and blessing, furthering the labours which should he the means of the salvation of men. He then spoke from the words, "Even there," " even now," "even so," showing that in the most unlikely places " even there" God's presence is with His people. The most desperate circumstanec was a time when "even there" God would nndertake for them, and in the darkest hour they could say" even so Father, for so it seemed good in Thy sight.' In the afternoon a united service lot the Sunday School, the Young Women's Bible Class, and the Men's Union was held. Special hymns were sung by the children and a special collection was taken up by boys land girls in aid of the Building fund. An interesting address was given by Bishop Eldridge on the use of the small and insignificant things in the service of God. In the elkning a large congregation listened to most impressive sermon by Bishop Eldridge who based his remarks upon the text John xx. 16," 'Rfibboni, that is to say, Master." He pointed out the frequency with which this title was applied to our Lord in the New Testament. Jesus Christ also 'aimed it for Him- self (John xiii. 13) and we found the disciples address- ing Him by it many times. Enquirers after the truth also gave Him this title, while some of His bitterest enemies addressed Him by the same name. Many called Him Master who did not belong to Him at , all. Judas as well as Peter and John spoke of Him and , to Him thus. Some who wanted to catch Him in His talk saii" Master " and "Good Msster"and multitudes in the present day Mg so, although in their lives they do not admit His Mastership. " Not everyone that saith unto Me Lord, Lord," eto. Oh ! the horror of saying Master and kissing Him in order to betray Him, thus showing that not in any real sense is He Master at all. Continuing Dr. Eldridge shewed the word translated , " Master" in our authorized version is from five different Greek words each having a distinct shade of meaning and suggesting a special idea, viz, teacher, such as a master of a school. This is what Jesus Christ was to the disciples of old. This is what. He is to-day. We are to learn of Him as our Master, Teacher, and allow Him to•awaken in us new interests in everything to which he directs our nilnds. Another shade of mean- ing is "A Leader." The Lord Jesus Christ is a guide who knows, and who shows the way. We have also a sterner word (2 Tim. ii. 21) which means the oespot, the Sovereign Master, one who has the right to com- mand our service, our absolute allegence. We are vessels fitted to the use of the despot, who can deal with each as he pleases, who can use it or break it, or mar it. In such a sense Jesus Christ is the Master of every individual Christian but such a Despot that it is the blessed privilege and right of every believer to allow Him to do with us what he will. This involves a surrendered will and a ready submission to what He may appoint even though His appointment may mean our disappointment. Another word implies a superintendent, one who stands over and directs another, taking all the responsibility. The last word was translated " Lord " a title of respect as well as of authority. The "Lord "who takes account. "To His own Master He standeth or falleth." The day is coming. when our deeds will be judged by Him. God grant that in that day we may he found faithful and •receivd thQ reward. The word" Master" existed in the Jewish Ilanguage in a threefold form Rab,-Master, Rabbi, my

Master and Itabbcmi,mv great Nists!-e,. So, Mary abplied to Him the title of, honour and love as great as could he found. , Christians should seek to copy her example in the very hi4.Theet sense in which it is possible for theni to take Jesus Cnrist as their grest beloved Master, the only Master. At the close of the service which was of a hearty and impressive character. nt persons partook of the [July Communion. Altogether the (las, will rank as a memorable one in the history of the church, the Bishop's discourses being very pewerful told creating a great impression. The large nongrevttions were an evidence of the flourishing condition of the churoh4

div.p: FIRES AT WARR;NGTON.
Family's Narrow ESG3,I3.

_ The shop of the faseds Spot Cash Tailoring Company.' 113, Sankey-street, Warrington, was gutted by fire in ,the early hours of Saturday morning. Toe premises were locked up at 8.33 on Fri(' ty night, and when a police constahle passed on his ronod at one o'clock the following morning they appaared to he as usual. At a quarter to two, however, Nix% Hewitt, veterinary surgeon, whose house adjoin and also extends over the shop, was awakened by a noise, and in a few seconds he heard a smash of glass, the shop window having burst with the heat. He jumped out of had, and on the stairs met his niece (Miss Pugh) making a hasty retreat. She, too, had beArr awakened by the crash of glass and then she saw. flames outside her bedroom window. This room is two storeys above the shop. At this moment a policeman rang the bell and warned the honse- hold to make e qnicklexit, as the fire had got a good hold in the shop, and smoke was entering the house. Mr. Hewitt, his mother (Mrs. Pagh). and 'his niece did so. The alarm was given, and the Fire Brig vie, under Superintendent Turner, turned out with the engine Captain, ladders and reel cart. On arrival they found the flames bursting out a considerable distance. Two jets were got to work from the mains—the engine riot being required—but the shop was completely burnt out in an hour's time. The strennonswork of the firemen resulted in .Mr. Hewitt's Premise i being saved, but considerable damage was done to the furniture. The origin of the fire is a ruystsry.

div.head: Oltbreak at BrFo2t.
div.p: Oltbreak at BrFo2t.
FIREMEN'S NARROW

Another serious fire occurred on Taesday morning at 12.15 on premises which have long been known as " Chrimes' Old Brewery," but which are now used as a warehouse by Messrs. J. liallwood and Sons, corn dealers, &c. rhe Fire Brigade was summoned by tele- phone, and a full complement of men, under, the direction of the Superintendent and Deputy Superin- tendent (Mr. Frank Turner, gen., and Nlr. Frank Turner, Jun.) were quickly of the scene with the steam fire enhine Captain, the fire escape, ladders and reel cart. Sergt. Evans and a number of other policemen were early in attendance, and made unsuccessful efforts to extinguish the flames. The fire-non worked hard, to prevent the fire spreading to the adjoining buildings, I including the historic " Old Academy" at Bridge-foot : and in this they were eminently .successful. Great damage was, however, done to Messrs. Flallwood'a ware- house. Part of the roof fell in, and the whole of the stock—bay, straw, wheat, oats, &c., the largest the ;firm have yet had—waS rendered absolutely useless by fire and water. The tire continued to burn fiercely for several hours, arid it was eight o'clock before it was so completely mastered as to .enable the hulk of the fire- men to return home for a well-earned rest. There were some horses in an adjoining stable, but they were safely removed as soon as the fire was discovered. I Several of the firemen had narrow escapes. One or ! two slipped while standing on the roof, but were saved by' their comrades. If they had fallen to the bottom ! they would have berm either suffocated or burnt to death.

How the fire originated is not known bat Mr. Hall- wood believes it to have beau caused by an incendiary. He estinattes his loss at over .ClOO, and though it is nearly covered by insurance it will he very great, owing to the dislocation of business end other reasons.

We should all return to the THE WHIR OF village life, Mr. G. K. WHEELS. CHESTERTON has been telling

a London audience. In this way, he seems to think, we should escape from the tyranny of wheels. This seems to us to be a very remarkable conclusion to arrive at in the present condition of things. Village life—for the whole habitations of most villages are by the roadside— is being made intolerable by that very tyranny of wheels of which Mr. CHESTERTON complains. Perhaps, however,when Mr. CHESTERTON says "all" he means all, which is everybody. If we lived in villages we should possibly abandon our motor- cars as well as our cotton factories and our engineering shops, our tramcars and our cabs. When the populations of our large towns and cities had taken to the simple country life there would not be any country left. Begland would be dotted over with villages easily within hail of each other. It would be one large town with the houses rather more widely distributed than usual, each, we suppose, with its garden and its orchard. We dare not say, each with its wheelbarrow and its mangle ; for if these were suffered to exist we should again fall under the tyranny of wheels. The idea of the beauty and simplicity of life in the country is one that appeals to all of us who live "in city pent." " God the first garden made, and the first city Cain," says the poet COWPER. The charm of life in the country is immeasurably great—to the spectator. To the inhabitants cf the villages it is not quits EO convincing, as a rule. There are model villages," but they are like angels' visits. They are models of what other villages should be and are not. Mr. ROBERT BLATCHFORD, supporting Mr. CHESTERTON, said that there should be a return to village com- munities of a kind where there would be very little law and where every lean had room to be himself. What we should ourselves like to see as a com- mencement is a sufficient provision of water-tight cottages, well-provided with modern sanitary arrangements, and having a roominess which was not dependent upon high rents. Then we might see people, if not going back to the land, at least staying upon it. A revival of the old cottage industries might follow, and an English village might become in fact what, we fear, it has been hitherto only in poetry and tradition. But what is the plain prose of the situation ? Some poetising cyclist discovers a pretty village, rather out of the way, where milk and bread and cheese are cheap. Ha—or more probably it is she writes to the papers on the subject, as if it were a new star that had swum into his ken. "Let US all return to village life," cry Mr. CHESTERTON'S disciples, and they do this, sending np the villagers' rents, drawing the simple folk from their proper occupations, and upsetting their lives generally. It is vain to tell us to go and live in the country, where we should have room to be our- selves. It is vain to hope to escape the tyranny of wheels. By wheels are our clothes being woven, our food distributed. Our civilisation is based on wheels. Cloth,as we know, can be made in cottages. It is made in rude cottages built on almost uninhabitable islands in the far North of Scotland. It is from there that the Harris tweeds come. What sort of lives do the weavers of woollen live? A few years since there was a fierce discussion as to whether Harris tweeds could be safely admitted into our households, so wretched, it was said, were the conditions under which they were made. Almost everywhere' under existing conditions, the pleasantness of village life is a dream. It has probably never been anything else. In Greece, Corydon and Phylli3, singing alternative passages of love-songs under the Greek equivalent for the hawthorn down in the dale, existed only in the imagination of Theocritus.
Some put the happy season further back,

Some forward. But suppose a perfect village life to be possible; how could it be possible for all of us? When Mr. CHESTERTON has told us that, he will have left the land of shadows and illusions; or is it, in reality, the old, delightful land of make-believe ?

Lord Lindley examining THE LAW AND THE the Deceased Wife's Sister's PRAYER•BOOK. Act, has found it necessary to explain, for the benefit of certain ecclesiastics, what is the precise position of the Ecclesiastical Courts in relation to the law of the land. During the passage of the Act through Parliament a great deal was heard of canon law, and the obligation of the clergy and the laity of the Church of England to observe the law of the Church as distinct from the law of the laud. Lord Lindley points out very pertinently that there is in fact no law, ecclesiastical or otherwise, except such as is embodied in the civil law. There is only one law-giving body in this country, the Parliament of the realm, and the only law which the Ecclesiastical Courts are able to administer is such ecclesiastical law as is sanctioned in the Statutes of Parliament. One

point of interest in this matter for the Church of England is in regard to the Prayer-Book. The prohibited degrees, as defined in the Prayer-Book, include the deceased wife's sister. But the law of the land has taken her out of the table, and the allegation at the head of the list that those named therein " are forbidden in Scripture and our Laws to marry together" is untrue. The alteration of the Prayer Book is surely a necessity.

At the recent Primrcse MR R. PIERPOINT League meeting at Penketh, AND CHINESE Mr. R Pierpoint made some ' LABOUR. interesting and rather amusing references to Cn.nese Labour—or quasi-slavery as our member so accurately describes it—in the Transvaal. Mr. Pierpoint waxed most unrighteously indignant with the Government for not having sent all the Cninese back aceorling to promise. He made thel suggestzo falsi that having been in office over a year, the Government had had plenty of time to repatriate the Chinese. Yet no one knows better than Mr. Pierpoint —and in another columul Mr. Crosfield, M.P., nails him down to the fact —that at the last minute before resigning officel his party issited 15,000 fresh permits for the employment of Chinese and fixed the indenture at the long period ot three years. "By taking these steps," says Mr. Crottield, " they deliberately made it impossible for any British Government to get rid expeditiously of the Chinamen, except at an enormous cost in compensation which wou!cl have been paid by the British tax- payer." And yet Mr. Pierpoint has the cool effrontery to tell the docile Primrose Leaguers that" people were now convinced that many of the members of the present Parliament were returned on terminological exactitudes or what in better English they called lies." It appears to us that some members of the previous Government also have arrived at a profound belief in the efficacy of a "terminological inexacti- tude" as a means to an end. We are sorry to find Mr. Pierpoint persisting in wilful misrepre- sentation, foe be has been challenged on this point before. Mr. Crosti&cl puts some very plain questions to him, but we do not anticipate that Mr. Pierpoint will reply. He has made charges which he cannot substantiate but in the interests of the politiCal honesty for which he professes to have some concern we hope he will refrain from their further repetition.
Interest in the naunicipal THE COMING elections is early being ELECTIONS. manifested. We have

already a brand new Liberal candidate in the field in the person of Mr. J. T. Locker, the recently-appointed hon. secretary of the Liberal Association. Mr. Locker is a well- known and popular townsman, and with regard to his candidature for Fairfield Ward we have only one regret, and that is that he steps into the shoes of Councillor Duncan, an old and tried member who is resigning owing to ill-health. Mr. Duncan has always been one of the quiet Coun- cillors, but he nevertheless did a good deal of valuable work on Committees and rendered special service in certain branches of knowledge. He posseses the respect of all parties, and regret will be general that physical infirmities should con.pel him to relinquish office. In Mr. Locker he would have a very worthy successor, and we hope the latter will be elected. So far there is no hint of opposition to him, but it is reported that our Conservative friends are going to make a desperate raid on the Liberal strongholds this November. They will find the tenants quite at home and fully prepared. Another candidate who is to the fore is Councillor Wilding. Dame Rumour, that lying jade, said that he did not intend to seek re-erection. The out-spoken member for Tcwn Hall Ward thinks'otherwise, and in one of our front-page announcements he asks his constituents to reserve their votes for him. Out of nine councillors who retire this November no less than eight are Liberals, so that the opposition will have its hands full if at all desirous of looking for trouble.

Fifteen hundred Warring- LIBERALS AT ton Liberals mustered for BELLE VIIE. the picnic to Belle Vue on Saturday and there was a consensus of opinion that the outing was one of the most successfHl on record. Not a single untoward incident marred the pleasure of the occasion and the six hours or more which were spent in the famous gardens did not hang at all heavily. The workers were delighted that Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P. and Miss Crosfield accompanied the excursion and a source of additional satisfaction was that the Member was looking very well after his short holiday in Switzerland. Speech-making had necessarily to be brief ,but Mr. Crosfield compressed into his address an interesting review of the more important legislative achievements of the Gcvern- meat. He had no difficulty in proving that Sir Henry Carnpbell-Bannernaan and his colleagues are bent on doing their utmost for the working- classes and already some extremely useful measures of reform have been passed. The Trades Disputes Act which strengthens the principle of collective bargaining, in which Mr. Crosfield is such a firm believer, has allayed the profound concern created in trade unionist circles by recent jndicial dscisions and has been welcomed by the workers all over the country. Mr. Crosfield rightly laid st.ess upon two great Acts affecting the land question, which really lies at the root of all social reform—the Land Tenure Act, aptly termed the" farmers' charter," and the Small Holdings Act, which it is hoped will do a great deal to encourage agricultural pursuits and arrest the constant migration from the country to the overcrowded towns. The Government's record is one of which Liberals have every reason to be proud and they may have perfect confidence that with our honest and determined Premier in cow 'nand .the progressive work will make rapid strides.

_lama= - Extremely sad iehe THE AFRICAN picture which the Bishop DRINK TRAFFIC. of West Equatorial Africa draws of the degradation and disease which are overtaking the natives in some of the colonies under the Bishop's observa- tion. Gin is used as coin of the realm in which labour is paid, and even then it is a dirty and poisonous hquor, against which Africa's children ought to be protected by a benevoient Govern- ment. It is an impudent and supercilious criticism to say that the African InstiVO needs to deal with temptation like everybody else upon this planet. The corruption of any condition of innocence—either in year or in experience—is a shame from which any creature of right feeling would naturally shrink. In tropical lands the devastation of" trade" gin does not stop on this side of calamity. The " nigger " who knows no better than to drink such stuff may be a meaner product of civilisation than the educated English- man who plies him with it; he is, nevertheless, entitled to consideration. No man can turn a Maxim gun upon these races except by a fitt of the State, and in point of responsibility the same may be said of this mischievous traffic. Restrictive measures need to be at once devised, together with a proper medium of exchange. The consequences to which the Bishop draws attention in the" Times "are reason enough for moving, and that quickly, in the matter. The burden of the Bishop's Christianising task should not be made too heavy ; and on his showing, when criticism has said all it can in mitigation, there is a casejnade: out for looking into this evil.

Sir James Crichton-Browne FOODS FADS. certainly deserves the thanks of the plain man who has no time to worry about diet, and who has been accustomed to take what an ignorant generation taught him was the proper thing for lunch—a chop or a steak. lii recent years the dietetic cranks have striven without ceasing to make his life a misery. They have told of all sorts of horrific perils lying concealed in the warent innocence of the coy cutlet or the chaste chop. They have wrung his withers whenever he had dine to look at the papers by telling him of all tilt) things he has eaten that he should have left uneaten and all, the things he has left uneaten that he should

have eaten. New steps in gallant Sir James, and with one fell swoop scatters the cranks and leaves the plain man free to enjoy his meat and drink without consulting a dietary table or a menu marked with letters to in3icate the presence or otherwise of "uric acid." We are among the plain men who have refused to be worried. We have eaten our chop in unrepentancerand have consumed our steak even under the eye of Mr. Eustacs Miles. As a matter of fact, the best guide to health in all feeding is moderation and reasonable variety. Rich things taken in abundance are bad —nature soon makes that plain. Food fads, as Sir James calls them, are well enough for people who have time to indulge them ; but they will not profit the majority, and the roast beef of Old England still has supreme virtues if taken in moderation.

The adhesion of Earl Cromer to the Unionist Free Trade Association is a not,ible fact which Tatiff Reformers .will not enjoy. That one of the ablest financiers among our statesmen who have carried weighty responsibilities for many years should be a convinced Free Trader is not to be disregarded. The Barings know as much about the economic conditions of trade as any men, and Lord Cromer cannot be set aside as an inexperienced authority. *

The "Warrington Guardian" report on Wednesday of the Liberal picnic to Belie Vue was peculiarly "neutral." Thel report waxed enthusiastic about the, animals in the Zoo, and about the quality and dimen- sions of the tea. Even the fireworks were described with copious detail, but of the important speech on current politics delivered by the Member for the Borough there was not a line. True, the report states that "the Member enumerated some of the principal measures, etc." But this is all. The remarks of Mr. Crostield, in. the view of our "neutral " contemporary, evidently rank in relative importance some way after the antics of the inhabitants of the monkey-house. Truly, a curious example of that hybrid type of journalism termed "neutral."

One of the Tory oratnrs in the Kirkdale hv-election had great difficulty in starting his speech. He began, in a confidential tone, thus: "1 want you all to go back with me in recollection for over a century." A roar of laughter was the response. Commencing again, the speaker said: "I know that lam younger than many of you," but, alas! the loud laughter was hereupon renewed. Pulling himself together for his third effort, lie said, with assurance, " Well, you will all remember the French Revolution of 1792." Of course, the audience laughed longer and louder than ever. Still persevering, the orator at last made his point. _
