Not very bog ago a broker went about all one day with an old Dutch picture in a barrow, trying in vain to sell it to well-known dealers for .-Z3. He took it at last to sell to a dealer not so well-known, who, how- ever, is a judge, and to him the picture was sold. The purchaser kept it a week, and then showed it to a. famous dealer, offering it for ;‘..:400. When the • , bargain was completed and the money paid over, the famous dealer said, "I can't help fancying I have seen this picture before, quite lately! " Yes," said the other, "you saw it last week in a barrow, and declined to buy it for three pounds! "—J. H. iOXALL, M.P., in "London Opinion." 5 The United Methodist Church, which has just been - formed, is probably the most independent religious...-. body in the kingdom. The Act of last session which • constituted the new body— so far, at least, as its property was concerned —avoided all reference to theological doctrines. It simply enabled the new body to place its religions tenets in a deed poll, and in that deed power is given for the revision both of the doctrine and the government of the Church at stated periods. The United Methodist Church therefore, dossesses the power of creed revision, and if it carries any change of that character in the prescribed manner, its property is safe from attack on the part of any dissenting minority. There is probably no other religious communion in the country that occupies so free and independent a position. 0 All the ridicule that has been poured forth on the ladies who indulge their pet dogs with luxuries beyond the reach of most human beings is doing nothing to stop the craze. More extravagant things are being dune than those denounced by Father • Vaughan or satirised at Drury-lane. Tailor-made coats and patent leather byots for the dear little pets have, of course, been quite the vogue for a long time, The coats are now provided for winter with collars of astrachan, or velvet lined with silk, and a lady is said to have paid five guineas the other day for a sealskin coat for her poodle. Fancy collars are an item upon which much money is spent, the present fashion favouring sky blue or red morocco with a smart satin bow, silver bells, and a charm. An American lady (says a London correspondent of the "Liverpool Post and Mercury ") even went the length of ordering a collar of solid gold studded with diamonds, at a cost of fifty guineas. "Goggles" for motoring d gs, toilet sets, medicine chests, and collap6ible bedsteads with the daintiest coverlets, are ameng the many other extravagances of the canine craze. * 0 0 The origin of the Chester Rows (they are unique in Europe) has long been a pretty mystery for the archmeloeists. Learned societies have listened to half-a-dozen theories at least, all mutually contra- dictory. There is the old idea that they are the remains of the porticoes of the Roman town -- which is patently absurd. Another notion is that the level of the Rows represents the level of the road in the old towns, and that the present street level is the creation of modern times; hut that won't do, because excava- tion shows that the Roman streets were on pretty much the same !eve} as these of to-day. A third theory is that the Rows acre coestractecl as street f .rtifica- tions to defend the people against the Welsh, but unfortuuately there is 00 evidence of the Welsh ever having been inside Chester. Borrow in " Wild Wales " gives this expLitetti n, and addsa picturesque description of how the Ches.er people fled upstairs into the rooms over the Rows when attacked. The other theories are more elaberate, but not wore con- vincing. The Rows are not mentioned before the fourteeeth century. In the next century we find a woman fined feurpence for tirineyin,.,e neighbours and passers-by in one of the Rows with the smoke from the tire in her " solar." * *

Warrington Free Churchmen will be interested to learn that on Monday, the Executive of the Council of the Evangelical Free Churches, decided that the Rev. David Brook, M.A.., D.C.L. (Oxon), the successor of the Rev. Silas K. Hocking at Southport, should be nominated to the presidency, for which the late Rev. Dr. John Watson had been chosen some time before his death. This nomination is, to all intents and purposes, an election. Therefore, Dr. Brook will, unless something very unforeseen occurs in the meantime, take up the duties of president next March. By a singular coincidence, the next annual Conference of the National Council, next March, was nearly twelve mouths ago fixed to be held at Southport. The selection of Dr. Brook is a tribute to the newly- constituted United Methodist Church, whose union was consummated only last week. Dr. Brook was probably the most prominent and best-known divine of the United Methodist Free Church, the larger of the thiee bodies which now b rat the United Methodist Church, and he has laboured unce,singly for a score cf years towards the union. Ile has just entered upou his seventh year ol ministry at the Duke-street United Methodist Chuich, where he has beim appeiuted until the year 191 g. Dr. Brook is at present president of the Liverpool and Distiict Free (Intel' Council, and also of the South-West Lancashile Federation of Free Churches. lie is wellinown in Warringtc n, having addressed public meetings here with great acceptance-

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
The Examiner, Saturday, September 28, 1907. SWITZERLAND.
ST. HELENS BLACKGUARDS.

Serious charges were at St. Helens Police Court on Monday, made against two respectable residents named John Barnes, insurance agent, Rigby-street, and Ellis Marsh, assistant chemist, Bickerstaffe-street. The offence was alleged to have taken place in the pit of the Theatre Royal on Saturday night. Evidence was given by a man named Doon, who lives in North-road, that the prisoners acted indecently towards him. Ho 'said that at first he thought the men were trying to pick his pockets. Afterwards he tackled Barnes, and took him ()Aide to give him in charge, and Birnes offered him money to settle the matter. Barnes pleaded guilty but Marsh denied the charge entirely. Both men were fined £5 and costs or two months' imprisonment.

div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
AUTUMN ASSIZES.
,e,4IMW

The Commissions for holding the Northern Circuit Autumn Assizes will open at Carlisle on October 21st; Lancaster, October 23rd ; Manchester, October 28th; and Liverpool, November 12th. There will be no civil business at Carlisle or Lancaster, but civil business will commence at Manchester at 11.30 and at Liverpool at 11 o'clock upon the thy following Commission Day, Commissioner Bray will preside in the Crown Court,and Mr. Justice Pickford in the Civil Court.

div.head: SCALDED TO DEATH BY COFFEE.
div.p: SCALDED TO DEATH BY COFFEE.

Mr. S. Brighouse conducted an inquiry at the Town Hall,Earlestown, on Wednesday, into the circumstances surrounding the death of Wilfred Wilson, the 12 mouths old son of Joseph Wilson, of 8, Sefton-street, Earles- town, who died on Sunday night as the tesult of being severely scalded by a can of boiling coffee. From the evidence it appeared that on Tuesday, the 17th inst., the child was left in charge of an elder brother,lo years of age, the mother having gone into the back kitchen for bread, leavins the can of boiling coffee on the table. Suddenly wriggling off his brother's knee, the child made a grab at the can and pulled it over, the contents falling over him and badly scalding his head and the upper part of his body. Dr. Latham was afterwards called in, and he attended the child up his to death, which occurred as stated. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. BRUNSWICK MALE VOICE cam.

The annual meeting in connection with the above choir was held in the Lecture Hall, Cross-lane. on Wednesday evening of last week,when there was a very good attend- ance. The chair was occupied by the President, Mr. J. C. Atkinson, who spoke very hopefully of the future prospects of the choir. The secretary (Mr. E. Goslin) gave a report of the past year's work, and spoke very highly of Mr. Turner's work as conductor. The follow- ing officers were appointed :—President, Mr. Atkinson; conductor, Mr. Turner; accompanist, Mr. T. R. Pres- ton, L.L.C.M.; hon. secretary, Mr. Ward, and a strong committee. The prospects of the choir are very bright, the membership numbering about 40. At a later stage refreshments were indulged in, and the Rev. S. C. Hall thanked the choir for the service they had rendered at his monthly meetings, and wished them every success in the coming season. 61111 MR. SEDDON M.P. AND THRIFT.

Speaking at a Labour meeting at Inc,e on Stturday. Mr. J. A. Seddon 'M.P.) said that when thirty-one mem- bers were returned to the House of Commons for the Independent Labour classes, someone had said, "Why, they have not even had a Liberal education, and not one of them has been to Oxford or Cambridge." No; but some of them had more dinner-times than dinners, and it was from such as they that the democracy could hope to realise the true measure of sympathy with their plea. The Grand Committee of the House,of Commons was very interesting. It was remarkable to find that a colliery proprietor was neither Liberal nor Tory there, but still a colliery proprietor. He had seen their member Walsh fight for two days like a tiger on behalf of the workers in the Compensation Act • in fact, the hand of Walsh was all over it. 'lf the Labour party had only secured the legal charter of the people, as trades unionists they had justified their existence. They had a Minister of War with £5,000 a year preaching about habits of thrift to a man with Hs. per week, and suggesting that he should qualify for the higher walks in life, and enter into competition with those with £5,000. Such ideas were not within the practicabilities of life. Thrift had better be taught to the man in receipt of thousands. Men grew old quickly in modern times, but they should not be condemned when old to the bastille known as the workhouse. The poor laws and the method of administration were brutal, cruel, and heartless. What they wanted was for the people to demand that the great Parliamentary machine should be used not so much for Empire-building, as the happiness of the people.

div.head: DISTRIBUTION OP PRIZES.
div.p: DISTRIBUTION OP PRIZES.

The prizes were distributed in the Lecture room at the Drill Hall, kindly lent for the occasion by Lieut.- Col. Edelsten, on Tuesday evening by Miss Trude Crosfteld. She said that she had very great pleasure in accepting the invitation to come and present the prizes which were verY handsome indeed. Although she knew nothing at all about shooting she took a great interest in the National Service League. She had been told that everybody present was a member of the league and she was delighted to see such a great number who had realised what ought to be done for the country which she did not consider to be perfectly safe under the present conditions. The objects of the League would put fibre and backbone into the physique and character of their countrymen. She thought the obstacles to the adoption of the League's principles could be summed up in three words—apathy, prejudice and suspicion. They found apathy in the .minds of people who were selfish and ignorant, and who would do nothing except for their personal ends. They, how- ever, found prejudice against their p i loinciples n the minds of some of the very best people in this country— most earnest people who had a prejudice because they were afraid lest national service should lead to aggres- sion. She congratulated the League on their successful competition, and wished a competition could be formed to give prizes to those who were most successful in persuading people to join their ranks. (Applause.) Mr. J. H. Smethurst proposed a vote of thanks to Miss Crosfield for her kindness in coming to present the prizes.—The Rev. W. Bracecamp seconded, ond it was carried unanimously. Inwood Moredaunt, aged 9, a lad who lived at Doonton-road, South Croydon, was cycling along the Pandisford-road, South Croydon, on Wednesday after- noon. He was knocked down by a motor-car and died in hosdital during Wednesday night.
CRAWFORD'S CREAM
C RACK E RS.
CRISP AND CREAMY
The Condition of the Workers and the Military System.
MR. J. ELWELL'S IMPRESSIONS.

With the object of seeing the Swiss military system in actual operation, a thoroughly representative British Committee of Inqiiiry, organized by the National Service League,, has just visited that picturesque land. As soon as the Federal Gove9- ment of Switzerland heard officially of the project it most generously offered to make the whole of the members of the Committee its guests during their stay in the country. Not only this, but the Govern- ment detailed a specially selected officer, Colonel Hans Pfyffer Yon Altishoven, to supervise all the arrangements for the tour, giving him at the same time assistants who speak English, and who accom- panied the committee throughout the tour. The following comprised the Committee : —Lord Ampthill, K.C.5.1., K.C.I.E. (late Governor of Madras, and Viceroy and Governor-General of India pro tern.); Lord Newton; Mr. John Ward, M.P. (Labour, Stoke- on-Trent) ; Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P. (Labour, Newton Division); Mr. J. T. Macpb.erson,M.P. (Labour, Preston); Mr. W. Hartley (Foreman Engineer, North British Locomotive Company, Hyde Park Works, Glasgow) ; Mr. E. Beauchamp, M.P. (Liberal, Lowestoft) ; Mr, G. D. Kelly, M.P. (Labour, South-west Manchester) ; Mr. Harold Cox, M.P. (Liberal, Preston) ; Mr. W, , Brace, M.P. (Labour, South Glamorganshire) ; , Alderman G. K. Naylor (London County Council) Mr. W. J. Morgan (proof-reader to " Birmingham; Daily Post ") ; gr. Joseph Elwell (A.ssociated Iron and Steel Works of Great Britain, Warrington) ; Mr. F. L. Joseph (City Councillor and Master Printer at Liverpool); Em E. E. Fiennes, M.P. (Liberal, Ban- bury Division, Oxfordshire); Mr. H. F. B. Lynch, M.A., F.R.G.S., M.P. (Liberal, Ripon Division, West Riding of Yorks).; Mr: A. G. Rickards, K.C., VD. : Mr. C. .S. Goldman; Captain G. R. Crosfield ; Hr. Frank Hader; Major-General T. Bland Strange; Major MacMunn; D.S.O. (" The Times ") ; Mr. Prevost Battersby (" The Morning Post ") ; Mr. Douglas Story (" The Tribune"); Sir Bartle Freie ("The Daily Telegraph ") ; Mr. George F, Shee, M.A. (Secretary National Service League) ; "Daily Mirror " ; Mr. J. B. Stubbs (Northallerton Miners' Association); Mr. R. B. Suthers (" The Clarion"). On Wednesday an " Examiner " reporter waited !upon Mr. J. Elwell, of Warrington, who was a member of the committee, and obtained some interesting impressions of the visit. Mr. Elwell paid a warm tribute to the hospitality of the Swiss Government who treated the deputation splendidly and gave them the best facilities for pursuing their inquiries. There were receptions in their honour and at lovely' Lucerne the festivities included a grand fireworks display. The tour embraced about one third of Switzerland and some of the most famous and beautiful 6p3t5. The military manceuvres were in' full swing and Mr. Elwell considered that the powers of endurance of the citizen army were remarkable, considering the short period of their training —a matter of 45 days. They entered into their work with enthusiasm appearing to regard it more in the light of a privilege than a duty, and in camp they passed much of their time in wrestling and other sports. 48,000 troops were engaged in the manoeuvres and the deputation saw the -principal ' operations near Belfaux. They witnessed the graad ' attack, the men engaged in it being under arms four' hours. Some of them had not been undressed for a, week; yet the way in which all :attacked was magnifi- cent. Another great event was the review of 30,000 troops, and Mr. Elwell said the movements were so admirably executed that the men were more like regular soldiers than civilians. He was also much impressed with the marksmanship of the shooting clubs:

At Berne, Mr. Elwell informed our reporter, the Committee waited npm representative Socialists and trade unionists and put to them a series of questions. One was as to whether they thought the military system had any injurious effect upon the trade unions of Switzerland. The representatives at first said the question was rather difficult to answer, but after dis- cussing it for some time they were agreed that the system had no bad influence upon the unions or upon , the industries. The period of military training wus so short (45 days the first year and IS days for subse- quent years) that it had no power to change the men's opinions. Another question was whether they would not prefer a voluntary system similar to ours, but they replied that the, would not, for the simple reason that it would place the control of the army in the hands of the capitalist. The citizen army was under the control of the people who therefore took a greater intereiit in it than they otherwise would do. The Committee inquired whether situations were kept open for the men who were engaged in military training, and were told that in the past the places had not been retained for the men, but of late years they had generally been kept open, except by the small employers. Some firms paid the .men half their wages whilst they were at camp. The Socialist and trade union representatives assured the deputation that they would not change their system for any other that was known.

Mr. Elwell also quoted the opinion of an elderly man, with whom he entered into conversation while watching cadets at drill, and who said : "If I had a hundred sons I would like all of them to go through the military training, for it • improves their physique and makes them better men altogether." The gymnas- tic schools which were so numerous in Switzerland did a very useful works Mr. Elwell thought the physive of the Swiss was scarcely equal to that of the British, but although they ,were not so stalwart in build the Swiss were exceptionally well develved across the shoulders.

The Committee had the privilege of inspecting some of the leading industrial eatafolishrnents including the machinery works of , -the Sulzer Bros., who employ 4,000 hands, and the loco- motive works at Winterthur. The conditions of the workers were about • equal to those obtaining in England and the wages for labourers-4s.a day—were better than the amounts generally paid here. The earnings of fitters and blacksmiths were about the same as in this country. The housing of the people was exceptionally good. Mr. Elwell went through one house, the rent of which was only per annum and which had a cellar, three rooms on the ground floor, three bedrooms and an attic. The hours of work per week were 57, Saturday afternoon being a holiday. " One thing that strikes you very forcibly in going' through Switzerland" said Mr. Elwell "is the industry of the people. Everyone seems to be working men, women and children. Every bit of land almost is cultivated. Peasant proprietorship is chiefly operative there and during the whole of our tour I don't think I saw half an acre that was nut under cultivation?'
Ur. Elwell also commented upon the extreme cleanliness of the people. The towns, he said, were practically without slums and were chiefly built on the

Rat system- . He did not see a fire-g-r-a-te—ail-t1;;;Q-1; was in Switzerland, the buildings being heated by means of pipes from the basement. 4 Neither did be seen any gas lights,electric lighting being the rule in the houses. The power was produced very largely by water. There was a good standard of comfort amongst the people and on going into France one cold not but he struck with the change for the worge in the appearance lof the houses, as compared with Switzerland.
" Switzerland" said Mr. Elwell "is more like a beautiful garden than a country." Giving his opinion of the Swiss military system, Mr. Elwell said it was the best that the Swiss could

have and if we in England had one on Somewhat similar lines we should be practically immune from any attempt at invasion. He would not, however, care to see the Swiss system adopted in its entirety. We should have the voluntary army system, with the comptqsory training advocated by the National Service League for home defence. We would then be able to reduce the standing army very considerably. He did not consider the system would be burdensome and be believed it would have a tewlency to make the people go_in for better conditions of life.

Mr. Elwell briefly touched upon the Swiss educa- tional system, pointing out that each Canton had self- government in the matter. Children were not sent to school until they were six years of age, and in some Cantons not until they were seven. They did not leave until they were fifteen or sixteen. Mr. Elwell concluded by remarking that he would retain pleasant recollections of everything connected with the visit, except the long hours. The Committee did not get to rest' until after midnight and had to be up between and 5 the next morning —which was fairly hard %yolk !

Readers of this column are invited to assist in making it interesting and helpful. to social workers by contributing themselves. Correspondents must write on one side of the paper only, and endeavour to make their letters and notes short and to the point. A nont-de-plume may be used, but the real name of the writer should be forwarded in confidence to the Editor of the column. M.S.S. must be addressed to John Workman, " Examiner " Office Warrington and should be sent in not later than Wednesday in each week.
CHRISTIANITY AND SOC;ALISNI. COLLECTIVE AS OPPOSED TO INDIVIDUAL

SELF-SA.CRIFICE. If I have to take up every point raised by other correspondents as well as those introduced by John Workman this controversy will become interminable. I am accused by a correspondent of casting a" slur" on John Workman, and the ground of offence seems to be a suggestion of carelessness on the one who edits a "Socialistic column in a Liberal newspaper." I don't quite know where the " slur" comes in, or why our friends should be so touchy, but if it be in that I have called a column headed the" Voice of Labour " a "Socialistic Coltman " I claim that my title is far more accurate that the one employed. The Editor is a Socialist, and every week uses the column as a pulpit from which to teach his creed. All his regular writers contribute Socialistic articles. If the opinions of those who differ are included, they only come in as strangers and aliens, and the Editor and his associates proceed to answer them from the Socialistic stand- point. I claim that' the present title is a misnomer because the thought in the contents only represents a minority of the world's workers,„and because it is almost entirely taken up with Socialist plans for the renovation of society, and little or no;hing is done to voice the opinion or aspirations of Labour. What place is made for the expression of the ideas of the large class of workers represented by the Trade Unions and the Co-operative and Friendly Societies, who do not happen to be Socialists? The title of such a column ought to indicate its character. As Socialists have started and monopolised this column, why then not give it a title which is really descriptive, such as "The Voice of Socialism ? During am interral in the first programme Mr. MACNAGIITEN, the head of the Macnaghteh Ntande- ville Circuit, introduced himself to the audience and said he wished to make a statement with reference to the policy he intended to pursue. He had come to ‘Varrington as a stranger, but he hoped he had come to stay. (Applause.) lie hoped also to be successful as an entertainer. He was addressing them in thitt beautiful theatre, the 20th which had been built in Great Britain. The foundation stone of the new- building was laid on the Ist May, and that was only the 23rd day of September, and they had had practically only four months in which to complete the work the audience now saw. It certainly reflected credit on their townsman, Mr. Davenport, who had done magnificent work. (Applause.) It was a work which spoke for itself ; his (Mr. Macnaghten's) work they would see in. the days to come. (Applause.) He was in a fortunate position in the matter of providing entertamments,as he controlled so many houses of entertainment, which put him in the position of providing the best talent the world produced. That was a figure of speech, no doubt in many cases, for every " showman " made a similar remark. Sometimes they gave the best show,sometimes they did not, but so far as he was concerned he would. provide them with an entertainment which he hoped they would appreciate, and he hoped to be able in the years to come to stand before them and receive their congratulations. (Applause). He would not take up their time by making a long speech; all he wished to do was metaphorically to shake hands with them over the footlights ; and tell them what he contemplated. He would specially cater for the ladies. (A Voice : "And it never fails.") It never had and he did not think it would. There were many ladies present that evening, and he wished to thank them for their attendance, because he often found when a person opened a theatre that they held back until they had heard from their male friends what the entertainment was like, and if it met with their approval they came. They had shown confidence in him that night, and it was a compliment he deeply appreciated, and he could assure them there would never be any item on the programme to which the most fastidious could reason- ably take exception. fie could not stay with them always, but his manager, Mr. Bradbary,would do every- thing that was possible in their interests, and if at any time there should be anything to which they took exception they knew where a letter might find him. If they wrote to him and told him what they wanted their letters would not be discarded and he would promise to answer theta with courtesy, and do everything to please them, and to popularize the theatre over which he had the honour to preside. He wished them all" Good- night," and thanked them very much for their attend- ance. (Applause.) The second house" was crowded to the utmost... and included a large number of guests of the manage- ment. The Mayo. and Mayoress and family odcapied one of the boxes, and many members of the Town Council and other well-known townsmen were present with their wives. The programme was the same as that submitted earlier in the evening, and could not have been better received. Mr. Macnaghten made another appropriate speech, in the coarse of which be said it was his intention to cater for the family—for ladies and children—all of whore would be welcome, and the entertainments would be such that the most iusceptible would not be offended. (Applause.) In conclusion, he asked them if they could say a word in favour of the Palace and the Palace entertainment. Let them follow the newspapers and advertisements, but he recognized that he stood or fell by what they said of him. If they would do so he would be established on a firm foundation. He would be quite willing to place the building at the service of the town for charitable purposes whenever it was wanted. (Applause.) At. this point a handsome floral bouquet in the shape of a horseshoe was handed to hr. Macnagliten, who said he thanked his friend, whoever he or she was, for his kind present. He regarded it as an omen of good luck. lie appreciated the spirit in which it had been given, and he would hang it lip in the entrance hall. It might not last very long, but it would serve as a. mealento of that occasion. Ho hoped it would bring the lack the anonymous donor meant it to bring to him. (Applause.) lhe proceedings ended at eleven o'clock, everybody voting the opening night to have been a great success. NEXT IVEEK'S PROGRAMME. Another at, ractive programrneha,s been arranged for aext week. John Tiller's company of 40 performers again head the bill and they will appear in a musical comedy extravaganza entitled "A Trip to Paris," which is certain to be highly a nusing.Bola Selvidge will figure as Hir nu P. Gibson from Cuicago and Jessie Templeton will take the ptrt of Camille Gibson, his wife. The first scene is laid in the Caatnps Elysees, a glade near le Cafe des Ambassadours and the second in The Moulin Rouge. Another brat class turn will be provided by Lawson and Namon, introducing comedy, trick cycling and ball pinching. Aracdonald and Huntington, American entertainers, 'tad Moon and Morris, clever comedians and simultaneous dancers,will also contribute to the entertainment. Raymond's bio-tableaux will show some new arid interesting pictures. Seats for the circle can be booked at the theatre from 11 to 3 daily.

CHARLES E. PARKER. Penketh, September 24th, 1907. " DEMOS " ON TEMPERANCE.

Sir,—Tri your issue of the 14th appears a letter signed " Demos " inviting Nil% Griffiths and his colleagues to define and defend Temperance principles and, being one of those colleagues, I take the liberty of indicting a reply to same. I am neither a fanatic nor an enthusiast but am a cold blooded teetotaler in my own interest and, feeling the beaefits I derive from it, I am not so selfish but desire to make known and extend its benefits to my fellows, for our Order enj ins upon us the duty of strengthening the weak and to lift up the fallen everywhere. I may remind "Demos " that it is possible to do an immense lot of gciod in the world without reading his catalogue of books. What is." Demos" hidden meaning in the fifth paragraph of his letter? What is he driving at in his reference to 18s. per week ? I have known men start careers on 183. and sometimes less and rise by dint of energy, temperance, and perseverance, to affluence and wealth. On the other hand, I have known men start careers on 'from .:t0 to £2O per week, who have, by dint of carelessness, drunkenness, and extravagance, brought themselves ; to poverty and the Workhouse. I know people in my own neighbourhood who have three or four times the income that I have who have most miserable and wretched hointis through the curse of intemperance. Will "Demos" not come on our side and help us to dry up this cursed stream of liquid fire from amongst us? Never mind the "old chestnuts." There are some good "new chestnuts" that will beat the old ones, and if" Demos" will join us and help in the good work, there is plenty of room in Warrington,and when we have reduced the drink traffic by 50 per cent. it will still be excessive compared with the average English town. —I am, Sec., I

div.head: :LOCAL BRANCH: BROGE ST., WARRINGTON.
div.p: :LOCAL BRANCH: BROGE ST., WARRINGTON.
LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE YOUNG LIBERALS ASSOCIATION.
Amalgamation Scheme Approved.

The autumn meeting of the council of the Lancashire and Cheshire Young Liberals Association was held on Saturday in the Manchester Reform Club, King-street. The president (Nlr. C. L. Williams, of Stockport) occu- pied the chair, and there was a representative attendance of delegates irom Liverpool, Manchester, Warrington, Stockport, Bolton, Oldham and Stalybridge. Mr. F. G. Lloyd presented a statement of the conference which had been held at Birmingham with the view of uniting the forces of the Young British Liberals Association and the National League of Young Liberals. It was felt that both societies hai one common end in view. and that the work xvoitid he more efficiently done if there was a unification of forces. The confereme agreed to a scheme of amalgamation, and a series of resolutions were submitted to the council for confirmation. After discussion the resolutions were agreed to unanimously, the purport of which was that all the societies at present affiliated with the Lancashire and Cheshire Young Liberals Association should on and after January Ist, 1908, he affiliated with the National League of Young Liberals. A letter was read flioni Mr. .1. W. Bogle (hon. secretary) stating that owing to ill-health he was com- pelled to relinquish the office. Regret was expressed at Mr. Bogle's illness, and a resolution of sympathy and thanks for his past services was unanimously agreed to. Mr. F. G. Lloyd, of Manchester was invited toll!l the vacant office of secretary, and he consented to do an. A discussion took place on the attitude of Young Liberals towards the House of Lords. A resolution strongly supporting the Government's action was passed and it was decided to keep this subject and other pressing social reforms well to the fore during the ensuing winter session. With the view of making the educational work of the societies more effective, a special committee was formed to organise a scheme whereby competent speakers who had made a special study of social subjects could place their services at the disposal of any society affiliated with the agsociation. A resolution was also agreed to advis- ing Young Liberals to take an active interest in municipal affairs.

div.head: WHITE CITY, MANCHESTER.
div.p: WHITE CITY, MANCHESTER.

Nothing is lacking in the way of entertainment at the WhiteCity,Ma.nchester. Joy and the good cheer of spirit reigns supreme everywhere. The Managing Director, John Calvin Brown has a number of novel amusement surprises in store for the patrons of the White City, and which will be announced from time to time. It can be depended upon that his best efforts to keep this amusement centre in the vanguard of the greatest resorts in Europe, will be put forth. He has aptly said that "In conducting any business it is necessary to have an ideal." This applies certainly to the .management of a summer park, and the White City as it now is, is the result of lofty ideals in the minds of those who planned it, who have fostered its growth, and who have made of it amost ideally perfect summer amusement spot. Ever since its opening the patrons have been educated educating them to expect more and more. They .now expect the standard to be raised higher and higher. Ever- ything of a mediocre nature is excluded, and nothing but the hest and most up-to-date features obtainable are sought. The hands are the very best in Great Britain, and for next week the full hand of the Royal Marines (Portsmouth Division) under the direction of Lieut. George Miller, M.V.0., Mus. Bac. Cantab. will furnish the music, by kind permission of the Colonel Com- mandant and Officers. In fact ' everything is on the same order. Those financially interested are congratu- lating themselves upon having a manager like Mr. Brown, whose ideals are high, whose self possession is a constant trait. , and whose executive abilities are far above the average. The whole of the Press are and have been unanimous in their praise of this unique and novel entertainment ever since its inception.

div.head: AUTUMN COLDS.
div.p: AUTUMN COLDS.

Reference has already been made to the increasing prevalence of the autumn cold. This, as our readers may be aware, is caused by the carelessness one has really no right to exhibit.in the face of such inconstant weather as we are tried with. But people will be care- less, in spite of all the advice in the country. Others, again. take cold in spite of every precaution they can think of. Do not neglect the cold. There is something to be said for the statement that every cold will last its time, but if one is not heedful bronchial complications of the gravest kind may ensue. It is, of course, advis- able to have always at hand a good and well-tried remedy, and this will be found in the following prescrip- tion. which will be dispensed by any chemist :—Syrup of Squills, one ounce; Karox Compound, one ounce ; ,Syrup of Virginian Prunes, two Ounces. It is claimed that this remedy has effected wonderful cures in chest and throat complaints.

Dr. Barnardo's Homes. The total amount realised in the house-to-house ! collection foi• Dr. Barnardo's Homes last Saturday, was £25 2s. The work of collecting was performed ' by the members of the eight Warrington Societies comprised in the Warrington and District Union of Young People's Societies of Christian Endeavour. The honorary local Organizer and Secretary was Mr. W. Worrall. LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER THE CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Adtv. Drunken Mother's Neglect. A shocking case of cruelty to a child was heard at , the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday morning when Satah Ann Miller, Watkin-street, was charged with neglecting one of her children, aged thirteen. It was stated that on Friday last the prisoner's , daughter was seen by Police-constable Lewis in ' Winwick-street crying piteously, and complained that she was very ill. The officer found on examination that the child's heal was covered with Vermin; a part ' of the skull being eaten away. Prisoner was addicted to excessive drinking, and neglected her home duties. The magistrates sent her to gaol for three months. Local Shepherdry. The .quarterly meeting of the members of the Late' Spring Rose Lodge No. 828, was held on Saturday at the Barley Mow hotel. A very creditable report of Ithe past quarter's working was given by the auditors, Bros. William Taylor P.-Nt., and George Ratcliffe. The amount paid as sick...benefit was 1..71 10s. The receipts exceeded the expenditure by 41 ls. 3d. thus bringing the total worth of the Lodge to £2,226 ss. 6d. At the close of the ordinary business Bro. Thomas Duckworth P.P.C.S. rtesenterl Bro. William Mather P.M. with a beautifully fruned emblem of merit, and spoke highly of the services rendered by him whilst passing through his office in the lodge. P.M. Mather suitably responded PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER THE CLOCK , FOR BERT BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Cycling Accident. At 9.50 on Saturday night, Sarah Molyneux, servant in the employ of Mrs. Worsley, the Cottage, Winwick was leaving the 'bus and crossing the road near the Swan Hotel, Winwick, when she was knocked down by a bicycle ridden by John Turner, 47, Leicester-street, Warrington, who came from the direction of the Hermitage. Molynenx was rendered unconscious, and P.C. Wooff, who witnessed the accident, carried her ida the Swan Hotel, where she was attended by Dr. Simps'in and Dr. Thompson; of the Asylum. Subsequently the girl was removed to the Warrington Infirmary in the borough police ambulance van, and it was found she was suffering from a slight fracture of the base of the skull. Death of Mrs. John Roge-rson. The death occurred under particularly painful circumstances at Bootle on Sunday evening of Mrs. Rogerson. wife of Mr. John Rogerson, stock and share broker, Market Gate, and Fcensee of the Griffin Hotel, Horsemarket-street. Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest on the body on Tuesday evening at the Bootle Police Buildings. Grace Davys, the tharried sister of the deceased, stated that on Saturday last Mrs Rogerson came from Warrington to step with her at her house at 00, Bank-road Bootle.. She was under medical treatment, and on Sunday afternoon, getting out of bed, she fell down the stairs, her head coming in contact with a flower stand at the bottom of the stairs. She was rendered unconscious' and died about four hours later. The jury returned a verdict of" Accidental death." Mrs. Rogerson, who was 33 years of age, was the youngest (laughter of the late Mr. Robert Innes PETROLEUM OM IN BARP,',ELS and Drums ' delivered free. Ask prices.—J. S. GARLAND, iron- monger, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Wycliffe P.S.A. An open meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society was held on Sunday. Mr. James Dodas presided and gave some very timely hints as to the Leeds of the present day. Be contended that instead of devoting too much time and thought upon the *New Theology" men should visit the poor, the slums and alleys of our towns, and get at the hearts of the people by helping them in their difficult surroundings. They would then be doing the work of the living Christ, who was always with them though they saw Him not with their natural eye.—The address was much appreciated. Many of the members said they remembered the address Mr. Dodds gave eleven years ago on "The centenary of Robert Burns, with lessons from his life." —Mr. J. Walley, of Manchester, gave an address, which was listened to with much attention, in which ha pleaded for greater regard for the place of woman in the world. Mr. W. Beswick read the lesson and Miss Fairhurst sang "Meditation " and "He was despised" in a most feeling and telling manner. Mr. W. Rutter skilfully played a cornet solo, Star of Bethlehem." The Secretary welcomed ten new members, making a total of-404. He moved a vote of sympathy with the friends of one of their number now lying dangerously ill at Winwick Asylum. FOR PURE PORK SAUSAGE, try ASILLEY'S.—Advt. Lancashlr3 Congregational Union.—Liverpool District. The autumnal meeting was held on Tuesday at Waterloo, Liverpool, when the presidential address was delivered by the chairman for the year, Mr. E. Shorrock Eccles, J.P. of Huytcn. His subject was "The present and future of Congregationalism." He remarked upon the altered social conditions and habits of the present day as not being altogether con- ducive to the spiritual prosperity and efficiency of the churches. Our Congregational churches are possessed of less wealth than was the case in the past. Their members pay more attention to sports and pastimes than formerly, somewhat to the detriment of public worship and Christian work on Sundays. He thought an alteration in some of their methods might be good. We are too isolated, and work too expen- sively; churches might be effectively grouped under one pastorate, and the gift of preaching be developed among our laity. There were also some churches which should boldly be abandoned as unretnunerative and wasteful in energy. He believed that the Educa- tion question would shortly compel closer co-operation among the Free Churches generally. The secular solution is the only equitable solution for the State, and the Free Churches must learn to act in combina- tion to impart religious teaching. (This declaration received the warmest assent of the meeting.) He further advoCated briefer pastorates, more Scripture reading in the services, brief liturgical exercises and shorter and brighter sermons. The address was received vgry heartily, and elicited considerable discussion. Woods' Great Peppermint Cure, for 'Coughs and Colds; never fails. 1/1 2/0. Local Successes at New Brighton. Warrington competitors acquitted themselves with greatcredit at the New Brighton Musical Festival, which was held on Saturday. The Warrington Apollo Male Choir, under the conductorship Of Mr. Harry Berrey, gained third prize (value £45) and silver medal in the male voice competition. The winners were :- 1, Manchester Orpheus; 2, Southport; 3, Warrington Apollo. The test pieces were " Where is He ?" (Beethoven) and " Myfanwy " (Harry Evans). The , adjudicators were Dr. Coward and Messrs. Harry Evans and Dan Price. The Lyric Quartette Party (Misses A. Woodland and L. Fairhurst and Messrs. IR. F. Cook and P. J. George) also added another to Itheir list of prizes by gaining first at the New Brighton lEisteddfod. There were 18 entries in this competition but only 2 put in appearance, and the unsuccessfull quartettes were unanimous in the opinion that thel Lyric thoroughly deserved the prize. The test piece was " Quando Corpus" (Stabat Mater) and the adjudi- cators, Mr. Harry Evans, Dr. Coward and Mr. Dan Price, said that No. 1 party (Lyric), had an excellent blend and the harmony was pure. The sotto voce parts were most beautiful to listen to and the chromatic parts were nicely done. In all it was a very fine performance and the judges had no hesitation in awarding No. 1 (Lyric) the first prize of LI 43. This local quartette party has now won over .£2O in prize money and four medals. They were specially coached for this competition by Mr. Harry lbrrey, St. Helena. It is also interesting to note that Miss A. Woodland. one of the above quartette party, had the honour of being chosen in the ,final for the soprano solo out of 28 competitors and although she was defeated the adjudicators remarked that she had a good voice full of rich tone. The trio competition attracted 11 parties and Misses A. Woodland, L. Fairhurst, and Mr. R. W. Cook were beaten by one point in the final. The adjudicators said that they had a beautiful blend and sang the piece with great feeling but he thought the tenor was rather weak and so they lost one point on balance. div.head: CRYSTAL PALACE BAND FESTIVAL.
div.p: CRYSTAL PALACE BAND FESTIVAL.
Crosiield's Band Compotes To-Day.

Warrington people will be interested in the great brass band festival which takes place at the Crystal Palace to-day, for the competitors will include Messrs. Crosfield's band. After a final rehearsal at the works the members of this fine band, which has done honour to the town at many important contests, left Warring- ton for London at 4.30 yesterday afternoon. Their fellow townspeople will wish them well in their efforts to capture the 1,00) guinea challenge trophy, for which eighteen of the best bands in the Kingdom will cort- pet°. Messrs. Crosileld's band, conducted by Mr. W. has been practising hard for this contest which will bring the season to a close. During the past few months the rehearsals have averaged four per week, so that after to-day's effort these enthusiastic bandsmen will be justified in taking a short holiday, from musical work.

To-day's festival promises to be a great success at least 150 bands will compete for £1,750 worth of prizes. and the contest for the 1,000 guinea challenge trophy will possess greater musical interest than that of any previous festival.

The test piece is regarded as being the most exacting yet set, and this forward step is rendered necessary by reason of the fact that the working men musicians of the North of England so nearly approach the pitch of perfection, that any ordinary test would make it very difficult for the judges to come to a decision. The selection for the leading 18 bands is from the composi- tions of Robert Schumann, the Saxony genius, whose end was so tragic. The movement opens with extracts from the overture " Hermann and Dorothea," into which the •' Marseillaise" is introduced as in the case of Tschaikowski's popular riot of melody "1812." This brines in a horn solo, which is followed by the cornets, and tries the players to the full. The euphonium and the trombone are later called upon for individual effort, while during the thirteen minutes concerted pieces bring in the fail strength of the six instrumentalist. in the final movement there is a splendid bit of brass band scoring, and the cl tssic selection closes with the last bars in the overture to "Julius Clessr."

In the various competitions nearly every county in England is represented, while Wales sends a dozen bands, Scotland one (Kirkcaldy Trades), but Ireland still lacks a friendly lead. Yorkshire heads the list with 25 organisations and the Lancashire competitors are Wingates Temperance (holders of the 1,000 guinea trophy and favourites for this year) ; Crosfield's Soap Works, Warrington; Goodshaw, Gossage's Soap Works (Widnes), Pemberton Old, Shaw, Colne, Blacksteads, Wrightington Suburban (Bolton), Morecambe Borough, Ashton-under-Lyne, Heywood, and Oldham, the three last-named being concertina bands, which will meet two from Heckmondwike and Mexborough. New Mills is Cheshire's sole starter.
, In past years some bands have been blowing away until late at night, but it is hoped that improved arrangements will see all the events ended about five o'clock in the afternoon.

It maybe of interest to players to know that all cash prizes will be paid by the Crystal Palace Company immediately after the announcement of the awards, and snecial prizes will be sent direct by the donors after they have received the official notification from the contest director. We understand that, Messrs. Crosfielcl's band is one of the five selected to play at the great concert with which the festival closes, and for this performance they will receive payment.

div.head: MAYORALTY.
div.p: THE MAYORALTY.
Alderman Smethurst Invited to Again
Accept Office.

A caucus meeting of the Town Council was held in the Town Hall, on Monday evening, to consider the selection of a Mayor for the ensuing year. The deputy Mayor (Alderman Bolton) was voted to the chair. On the motion of Alderman Bennett, seconded by Coun- cillor Toole, it was unanimously decided to invite Alderman Smethurst to accept office for another year, and a denutation, consisting of Aldermen Bolton, Bennett, Pierpoint,Tinnion and Forshaw, was appointed to wait upon his Worship, to convey the decision of the meeting to him, and to obtaia his consent to serve again. The qnestion of the retiring Aldnrmen—Messrs. Smethurst. Forshaw, John Evans, R. W. Francomb and Bolton—was also taken into consideration. A long discussion ensued, and it was proposed that the question be deferred till the annual meeting of the Council to be held on Saturday, November 9th. An amendment was submitted that the date be November 4th, but on a vote being taken it was found that the original pro- position had been carried.

Now the holidays are over, my members are sending me more contributions. Well, I am always pleased to receive them. I rau,st thank Harry Copp for several anecdotes, etc., he has lately sent me, and aleo many thanks to new members, Florence. and Doris Kivell, ~for contributions received.

How are you getting on with the Account of Holidays Lssays? Don'A forget that these must be sent in by the end or September, if you wish to win one of the prizes. Do you remember that last winter ,we had a special competition for working for the poor? I had many nice warm scarfs sent me, and can't tell you how pleased some of ray poor people were to get them. It's very, commonly said that we are to• have a sharp time, and, this, you know, will mean much ,suffering by those poor people who are unable to obtain much clothing. I am sure that all•of you have a soft spot :In your heart for those children less fortunate than. yourselves. I want you to be generous. and try and remember how many good things you have, .then see if you cannot help at least one 'poor child during our long wnter. Well, I won't say any more on this subject at the present time, but I should much like to receive postcards from those who are willing to glive me a little hell; during the winter months in providing • a few nice warm artieleo for the poor. - With love, from
UNCLE NED.
LoOk further down this column .for an ac- count of a very pretty novelty I recently saw in a shop window.
A STARTLING NOVELTY.

\ A week or two since I was walking through o?te of the principal streets of a large town. About twenty yards away a crowd had gathered, completely blocking from view a large window belonging to a grocer. Of course, I had to push my way through the people, and then saw a frame set back in the window ourrounded by a large stock of Neave's Food. Inside the frame a picture was painted on glass, and, strange to say, on Watching this picture a poor little thin child—hardly any- thing but bones—gradually grew plump and bonny whilst eating Neave's Food. The whole effect was most striking. I cannot tell you how it was produced, but it must have be€n by some mechanical movement behind the glass. On making inquiries I was told that the proprieters of Neave's Food—Messrs. J. R. Ner,vE and Co., Fordingbridgeare supplying these modelsl.to grocers and chemists for exhibition in their shop 'windows. The-one I saw was proving a tremendous at- traction. I hear that Messrs, Neave have another very -clever window model; if I come across one in my travels I wri:l tell my mem- bers all about it. lINCLL NED.
WHY TEDDY DIDN'T GO

"I'm going to run away," said Teddy to Dick. "I'm going over 'to my Aunt Nelly's house." Teddy wa,s a very little boy. He wore a kilted skirt, and he couldn't speak all of his words quite plainly. But he knew better than to run away; -because he whispered to Dick CO mamma wouldn't hear. Dick was a great black New- foundland dog. He was a year younger than Teddy, but he pas enough bigger to make up for that. He looked Up at Teddy as if he understood. and followed him off the verandah and around to the back gate. "Don't go far, slear," called mamma after them. Surely Dick understood that. He stopped waving his- plumy tail. "No—o, ma'am," said Teddy. But he put his hand on the gate. Do you suppo2e he meant to go jut the same? "Mamma said not to go far," he whispered to Dick. "It isn't far to Aunt Nelly's. It isn't • mer 4 than a rr.ie, D:ek; and che'll make us some toffy.' Teddy pushed the gate open. And what do yon
'f cr,

currose Dick did? Why, he laid himself down in the gateway; and when Teddy tried to step over him he growled dreadfully and showed all his white teeth. Teddy ttied coaxing, but Dick wouldn't be coaxed. Then he got. a maple cwitch, but Dick wouldn't be driven. Then Teddy tried to climb over the pickete; but Dick caught hold of the hiked skirt with hts teeth, 'and held him back. So at last Teddy made up hi mind that he didn't really want to go to Aunt Nelly's house. But he couldn't hell) telling mamma all about it. It was so funny. Mamma smiled, and patted' Dick'6 great black head. "Then it was My dog who minded,
and
not my little boy," she said. "But I'm going to all the rest of the time," said Teddy, earnestly.

Your burden is heavy, I haven't a doubt, But others have loads they must carry about, And-they are not whining. . Some people are glad if but half of the way Lies out of the shadow, or part of the day They see the sun shining. Suppose you try smiling. I know you are lonely; but other hearts ache, And bravely refuse to be bitter or break

Lymni Baker Again in Trouble.

At Prescot Sessions on Tuesday Thomas Thornton Gregson, baker, Lymm, was charged with being drunk in charge of a motor-car, and With failing to produce a licence to drive, and with driving a motor-car recklessly. All the charges were taken together, defendant pleading not guilty. Superintendent Bnxendale stated that about 4.30 on the 4th inst. a tramcar was entering the points of a loop at Horns Smithies, Huyton, from the direction of Knotty Ash. The driver noticed a motor-car coming in the opposite direction at a furious rate on the wrong side of the road. ,As the motor-car was abont ten yards from the tramcar the driver of the motor turned his car right across the road, and 'crashed into the tramcar. The motor-car was smashed in front and the wheels torn off. It was seen that the defendant- was drunk. A constable came up, and noticing the motor driver's con- dition, brought him to the Present Police Station,where he was examined by a doctor, who said he was not sober nor flt to drive a inotor-ear. - - --

Defendant denied that he was drunk. They only stopped twice during the run from Grappenhall to the place of the accident. He was a cripple, and did not walk steadily. A chauffeur named Tomlinson and a friend who 'accom- panied defendant corroborated the latter's statement. Superintendent llaxenciale said defendant bad been convicted on fiveilifferent occasions for similar offences all in connection with motor-cars.

The Chairmn said defendant would he fined 40s. and costs in the first case, `.2os. and costs in the second, and Vi and cor.ts in the third. They would endorse the licence, and also suspend until the end of February.

div.head: Illarrington Beat Runcorn.
div.p: Illarrington Beat Runcorn.

The popular fixture with Runcorn on Saturday attracted a great crowd to Wilderspool, there being fully 7,000 spectators. Beautiful weather prevailed.and with the ground also in perfect order there was every- thing to favour a fast game. Both sides were as selected, and the Runcornians were well supported by a contingent from across the river. The start was delayed owing to the non-arrival of ,Lees, and in fact the Warrington men turned out a man short, but the skipper soon appeared. The teams and officials were : Warrington : They, back ; Fish, Isherwood, Taylor, and Dickenson. three-quarters ; Lees (captain). and Brooks, half backs • Thomas, Boardman, Preston, Naylor, Heath. and Belton, forwards. • Runcorn : Harrison, back; Deakin, Batterworth, Moran, and Flanaghsn, three-quarter hacks ; Jolley-and Watton, half backs: Padbury, Leyland, Richardson, Walker, Dixon, and MacDermott, forwards. Referee Mr. F. Kenpedy (Broughton). Touch judges, Messrs. W. Mainwaring (Salford) and H. Ball (Wigan). Warrington won the toss. and Richardson started the game against a slight breeze. Runcorn soon showed , smartness in the front rank and Brooks bad to mark twice in order to check an invasion. On Lees arriving he took the place of Thomas behind the scrum .and Warrington at once began to show marked superiority. Harrison stopped a great forward rush in brilliant style. Warrington handled . smartly and Dickenson twice got dangerously near only to be stopped by Flanagban. The first score was not long delayed, for a weak kick by Moran left the home forwards in posses- sion and Heath dribbled over with the first try. Thomas failed at goal. Playing full of confidence Warrington still waned their aagressive tactics, and though Runcorn struggled hard they could not escape their quarters. The übiquitous Jolley was ever in the thick of the fray, but the rear line was weak, and the poor fielding let in Warrington again, Fish making a desparate but futile attempt to cross at the corner. Lees and Brooks were ' generally in possession, and fter several rather stiff scrimmages had been witnessed near the Runcorn posts. Lees suddenly darted away towards the left touch. All were anticipifting an opening for Fish; but evidently it was a movement preconvinced. for the Warrington skipper suddenly turned towards the open, and sending on to Brooks this clever player handed on to Dickenson, who took the oval at full speed and scored brilliantly. It was a clever try, and well men i ted the applause which greeted it. Thomas again failed with the goal kick. A sharp rally by Runcorn caused- Warrington to fall back, and Watton tried to break through, but failed to escape the vigilance of Brooks. Again was the weak- ness of Runcorn apparent when the rear line allowed Taylor to snap a pass intended for Moran, and tracks were made for the pavilion goal. Now that they had again established themselves here the ball was con- stantly swung out into the open, and after Lees and Taylor had handled, Isherwood nipped between Butter- worth and Flanaghan and scored spendidly after a strong run. Preston was entrusted with the place, and the kick gave Warrington a lead of eleven points. Butter- worth tried hard to put a better facing on Runcorn's record when he ran to mid-field. Tilley intervened,and directed operations to the Runcorn quarters, where Moran wss once more at fault, and Lees and Dickenson indulging in a combined passing run, tile wing man was almost a scorer•when Harrison stayed progress. A plucky effort by Watton was well seconded by his for- wards, and Runcorn, for the first time in this half appeared dangerous. Isherwood saved well near the line and relief only came when Lees and Brooks got away and directed operations at mid-field. Once more the Runcorn right wing was at fault and the blunders now becoming infectious, Heath took advantage of a had mistake by Jolley to score the last try of this half. the goal kick this time proving a failure. The interval was now reached with Warrington leading by one goal four tries (14 points) to Runcorn nil. The visitors had the benefit of the breeze during the last. half, and at once made tracks for the Warrington goal, Padbury being early conspicuous with a fine dribble, which was stopped by Fish. Isherwood tried bard to regain the lost ground, only to.see Harrison in magnificent form, and the play of the Ri.ncorp custodian at this period was a special feature. Runcorn continued to plod on, and they certainly deserved a score when Jolley dodged through, but met a fatal barrier in Taylor. Passing was tried by the Runcorn brcks, Watton opening out the game towards Deakin, who was safely knocked into touch by Fish. Another spell of safety play. with Runcorn the agresnors. was witnessed, and eventually the monotony was relieved when the Ruucorn vanauard svith Walker and Richardson as leaders, caused Warrington much anxiety. Isherwond again proved himself a most resourceful player when he effected a fine relief, and lodged the game at centre field. Passing between Watton, Jolley, and Butterworth placed the Runcorn supporters on good terms with themselves, and the old centre three-nuarter just lacked sufficient speed to make the try, for Fish raced up and tackled safely. The Linnets continued to have the best of matters, their forwards playing a robust game, and compelling Warrington to adopt strictly defensive tactics. Runcorn dribbled to Tilley, cho was penalized for not playing the hall promptly, and though the place was fairly easy Jolley failed to land the points,' much to the chagrin of the visitors' supporters. Final: Warrington, 14 points ; Runcorn nil. 1

div.head: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.

• PURIFICATION OF WATER BY OZONE. In the Cen(ralblat for Bacteriology, D. Rivas gives some notes on the purification of water by ozone. Under ' favourable condi- tions, he has found that the numb A.: of bac- teria are reduced by its action, and that the dangerous "Bacillus coli communis " is eliminated. It was also found to oxidise ammonia-forming nitrates. When, however, the water was rich in organic matter, the germ-killing and chemical actions of the ozone were only partial. The writer con- siders that purifica Fon by ozone is a favour- able method for th treatment of a town supply. Details of the methods of obtaining and applying the ozone are given.
CHEMICAL ENGINE FOR MINE FIRES.

For fighting fire in its anthracite coal mines a new form of chemical fire engine is used by the Delaware, Lackawanna, and Western Railroad. This engine is built on a truck which ' can run upon tracks throughout the mine.- When an alarm of fire is sounded the engine is attached to an electric mine locomotive, and rushed t 4 the scene of trouble at high speed. Water played upon a coal fire is almost instantly converted into steam, which further disintegrates, forming a gas so suff6'ating that it drives away the men fighting the fire. Blue flames which shoot out when water strikes the hot coal often set ablaze pockets of gas in the ceiling. When a chemical engine plays upon burning coal the heavy gases evolved cling to the floor and smother the blaze _ by. excluding the air. Men are not annoyed by the fumts, and can stay close enough to do effective work.

div.head: SPLASH OF A DROP.
div.p: THE SPLASH OF A DROP.

Professor A. M. Worthington, F.R.S., of the Royal I\Taval, Engineering College, Devon. port, read- a paper at the British Associa- tion on "An Unrecorded and Remarkable Feature in the Splash of a Drop." A drop of water falling into water, he said, ex- cavated a perfectly spherical hollow in the water. The hollow reched its greatest depth approximately at the same time that the water thrown up attained its maximum height; but the volume of the pit was enor- mously greater than that of the water thrown up, being SCO times as great with a height of fall of 197, centimetres, and 44 times as great with a fall of 40 centimetres. The original liquid of the drop lined the hollow cavity in the form of a thin layer. Surface tension appeared to play but a small part in this phenomenon.

div.head: SEAWEED'S CHANGE OF HABIT.
div.p: SEAWEED'S CHANGE OF HABIT.

In the Journal— of the 'Royal MicroAcopi- cal Society, Mr. A. D. Hardy gives an in- teresting account of a remarkable change of habit in a species of alga. The species in question normally inhabits stone-paved gut- ters with a rapid flow of water, or fast-flow- ing streams. It grows on submerged twigs of willows, and stems and leaves of water plants, but is more frequently found on stones or dead twigs. It was found by Mr. Hardy on the backs of gold-fish living in a pond. And while on the backs of fish it was growing luxuriantly, it was also found poor in quality on the stems and leaves of plants. "I think," writes Mr. Hardy, "that some in- terest, therefore, attaches to the adaptation of this stream-loving myxonema, which, find- ing the almost stagnant water of the pond unsuitable, had, by means of its zoogonidia, obtained a footing, either by accident or de- sign, on moving objects, thus obtaining the desired , water-friction to whicli the species had been accustomed." The interesting fact is added that from one small tuft of this species growing on a fish nine other species 0f algre were obtained.

div.head: MIRRORS MADE OF COPPER.
div.p: MIRRORS MADE OF COPPER.

The silvered mirror is commonly used be- cause of the faithfulness of its reflection; but many experiments have been made with a view to finding other metals which were susceptible of depositions on a glass surface.' Other metals can be deposited, but not , evenly and coherently, and hitherto one of the failures has been copper, although from its close relationship to silver good results from it would appear probable. Faraday found a method, but not a very successful or cheap one, and the copper mirror has hither- to been an expensive curiosity. Mr. F. D. Chattaway announced at Leicester, however, that in the course of an investigation of the aromatic hydrozeneS lie found that when copper oxide is acted on by these substances the copper can be deposited on glass in a thin coherent film. The mirrors obtained by such a method are, he adds, very beautiful, for they shew the lustrous red colour of pun nished copper, and are as perfect in reflect- ing surface and as uniform in texture as the similar mirrors obtained by the deposition of silver.
PORTABLE WIRELESS APPARATUS.

According to the Elektratechnik und 211c.!- cltinenbcru, the „United States • Army is being equipped with a light, portable, and compact wireless telegraphic outfit which can easily be transported on pack animals. One 2 kw. dynamo is provided for each army division, which can be driven by a spirit motor. This . dynamo weighs 135 kilos, and will be carried in one of the horsed waggons belonging to ; the ordinary baggage train of the division. Tho. transmitter and receiver are distributed amoni!st the various companies. Each group, of apparatus weighs no more than 140 kilos, ] and is so arranged as to be carried by a pack horse. They comprise the two elemerfts of the accumulators, which are charged for ten hours' working, ten sections of a mast which, put together, make an antenna 18 metres high, arid the receiver and transmitter. The latter are constructed for a workable radius of from 25 to. 40 kilometres. Fessenden's elec- trolytic detector is used in the receiving in- strument. It •is stated that each installation can be placed together and put into working order within about twenty minutes.

div.head: DOUBLE PERSONALITY.
div.p: A DOUBLE PERSONALITY.

Ome .of the most remarkable cases of double personality on record is described by Professor Pierre Janet in his work on "The Major Symptoms of Hysteria." ,The patient,. whom he calls Marceline, first Came to him about twenty years ago. For several months she had not taken any food, and was on the verge of starvation. After trying other methods of treatment she was hypnotised, and a secondarrlstate was induced, which, although apparently artificial, differed alto- gether from the state in which she hail been on her entrance to the hospital. She imine- diatelv began to eat, and soon rezained her strength. When she seemed on the road to recovery it was thought

div.head: NECESSARY TO AWAKEN urn,
div.p: NECESSARY TO AWAKEN urn,

from the hypnotic state, which was con- sidered artificial. Immediately the patient fell back into her preceding state. She was again unable to eat, and in order to save her life it wae necessary to reinduce the hypnotic state. . _
--7;-- The same experienco was repeated over and over again, and, as Professor Janct ex- plains, " things continued in this way for fifteen years. Marceline would come to me in

ORDER TO BE PUT TO SLEEP, • enter into her alert state, and then go away very happy, with complete activity, sensi- bility, and memory. She would remain, thus for a few weeks; then, either slowly or sud- denly, in consequence of some emotion, fall back into her numbness, return to the state we had considered primitive and natural, with the same visceral disturbances. The for- getfulness now extended over whole years, *lna disturbed her existence comuletely. She would hasten to come to me to get nersett transformed again. Things continued thus for years together, till the death of the poor girl, who succumbed to pulmonary tuberculosis."

It is evident thatlands' Football Club is increasing in prosperity and popularity, a crowd of almost 4,000 witnessing their match with the famous Everton com- bination team., which was plaved on the works recreation ground, Gorsey-lane on Mond2y evening. The enter- ; prise of the Warringtonians in arranging the visit is deserving of warm praise. The opening phases saw ! Rylands' attacking persistently. and their efforts were awarded by a goal from Daroysltire. who took advantage of an opening, giving Sloane no chance. After this the I Evertonians indulged in some pretty forward work 1 Jones. Cook, and Wood giving the home defence a troublesome time. Eventually the hall came out to Macconnachie, who took &liberate aitu and completely i surprised Baines with a shot which travelled under the bar. This succes was only the 1 forerunner of others, for Adamson added a ; second shortly afterwards. A particularly smart save was effected by Baines in coping with a shot horn Rafferty. No further scoring took place prior to the interval, when Everton led by two goals to one. The second half was greatly in favour of the Blues. Jones threaded his way through and scored a third goal, and a fourth was notched by Cook. For the homesters, Newton an Webb defended pluckily, tut the smart comLination of the visitors eventually overplayed them. Result :—Everton 4 goals, Rylauds one. DINNER AT TIIE LION HOTEL.

In proposing the toast of the " Everton team," the CHAIRMAN said there was no need for him to introduce the name of the 4'verton Club for it was known Ihroughont the length and breadth of the land, and in certain of our Colonies. AS far as their little venture was con- cerned, he thought that the works team might take a certain amount of encouragement from the history of the Everton Club. He remembered- that at one time the Evert= Club was in a very poor condition indced. The gentleman who would'respond to that toast would he able to confirm the fact that some twenty or twenty- ilve years ago their finances were not in the flouris.hing state that they were at the present time, lie hoped that they would always keep in their present prosperous position. Their example that day would no doubt prove of great value to ttylands' Club and he hoped R 3 lands' would strive to copy them—(hear, hear)—aud that they would win the medals and be the leading club in the town. Association football was absolutely on the go" in Warrington and he could tell that frora the way in which their own club 'had progressed. div.head: Chinese Labour.
div.p: Chinese Labour.
The Member and Mr: R. Pierpoint.

- -- Sir,—l observe that in a recent speech in the "Newton Division Mr. Pierpoint Made some rather strong remarks about the Chinese problem in South Africa. I confess to be rather at a loss as to what be is driving at. Does he condemn the employment of Chinese in South Africa, under conditions which are now notorious? In that CARP, one may fairly ask who introduced them? They were introduced by Mr. Lyttleton when he surrendered to the demands of those cosmopolitan financiers who regard (and who have treated) the British flag as a mere commercial asset to be used for their own purposes. Mr. Lyttleton, when he made this disastrous experiment had the suPport of the Tory party, including Mr. Pierpoint himself. Now, as a matter of fact, do on, Unionist friencis in Warrington think the Chinese Compounds a healthy system ; one that should help to form the permanent foundation of our new Colony in the Transvaal ? If that is their position weslmllhe quite ready to join issue with them upon it. I think we are entitled to know from the authrmised srokesmen of the Party especially when they Rina• criticism Out co freely what their position really is. P-Iss, Piernoint mean that he would like to gem the syqteffi of Chinese quasi slavery a permanent institution in South Africa? Or doe.; he admit that its introduction was a big and a bad blunder? As far as I can make out Anything clear at all fr,m his speech, Mr. Pierpoint seems to be vexed with the Liberal party, because we do not get the Chinese out of Africa more speedily. But if the Tory party wanted the Chinese sent back so quickly, why did they issue 15,000 permits to the Mine Owners just before they resigned office; and why diri they fix the term of indenture at so long a period as three years ? By taking these steps they - deliberately made it mpossible for any British Government to get rid„ expeditiously of the Chinamen, except at an enormous cost in compensation which would have been paid by the British taxpayer. In the last two months 4,000 coolies have been repatriated to China, and 15,000 will have left South Africa by Christmas. By the end of next year it is calculated that every Chinaman will have returned to his own country. • This has doubtless been a struggle with powerful interests, and there are those in the Progressive Party who have naturally chafed at delay; but I submit the event has shown that the Government has acted wisely in allowing the Colony itself to decide the matter. It was well to allow the electors of the Transvaal an opportunity of declaring in unmistakable terms their hostility to the ordinance. I recommend these facts to Mr.Pierpoint's attention. If he will carefully consider.them possibly the next time he refers to Chinese Labour his criticism of the Government's action may not be quiteAo wide of the mark—and of the facts.—Yours etc., A. H.
