div.head: Swiss Military Training.
div.p: Swiss Military Training.

Sir.—At the National Service League smoking concert last Tuesday I had the privilege of giving a brief out- line Of what the British Committee of Enquiry into the Swiss Military System saw during its recent visit to Switzerland. As it may he of interest to some of your readers to learn what manner of training the Swiss citizen undergoes, I venture to trespass on your space to supply, rather more fully than was possible in a speech, these details. To appreciate the effects of the Swiss Militia it is well to remember that Switzerland is but half the size of Ireland ; that its population is only a little over three million and of this 70 per cent are German. 25 per cent French and 5 per cent Italian, and that it is composed of 22 separate little states or cantons which, while jealous of their own rights, are loyally patriotic to the confederation as a whole. By law every Swiss is under the obligation to render military service. The physical standard for the army is however exceptionally severe and only 58 per cent. are passed each year as fit to hear arms. The rejected ones have to pay a tax varying from 69. 3d. to £l2O annually. By this means half the cost of the army is defrayed. Not a bad plan either and one that would considerably help the army estimates in this country. Military training begins in some instances at the early age of 14. Municipalities have the right to raise cadet cOrps, service in which is voluntary. Only some towns avail themselves of this authority and opinion is divided as to the advantage of beginning so young. of course the training is very mild. Two or three hours per week. But where there is subsequent training at the military age, cadet corns are not so important as where there is so little adult service as in our case. Boys remain in these cadet corps up to the age of 16. We saw some of these brave !ale fellows swim the Rhine at Bale, where the river some 200 yards wide, flows swift and strong. People are fond of saying that compulsion would at once put a stop to voluntary effort. This is not the casein the Helvetian Republic. From the age of 16 to 20 there is voluntary training consisting in drill, rifle exercises, running, jumping &c.. and about 30 per cent. of the youth of the nation enrol themselves in these volunteer corps which, so far as amount of training is concerned, correspond to our own volunteer corps except that there is no camp. But a further proof, and one perhaps more striking of the voluntary spirit, is the time devoted by men in order to become officers. in addition to the initial training of recruits which lasts 46 days for the infantry, and a ivolild-he lieutenant must put in about 200 days' training at different schools of instruction. Now no man is compelled to be an officer, therefore his extra training is entirely voluntary. At the age of 20 tee Swiss lad is sent off to his local school of military instruction. We saw one of these schools at work out in tt.e field, and here let me say that the kindness of the Swiss Government cud their representatives, Colonel Pfyffer, Colonel Camille-Favre, Major Vonwiller, Captain Meyer and others, was ove- whelming. We were allowed to see everything and everybody. We were the guests of the Federal Govern- ment, whose hospitality was lavish. The best hotels,the finest ssaloons,the toughest of motor-cars—they needed to be tough,for at times it was more like galloping to hounds than sober respectable motoring. As the representa- tive of the" Clarion" writes "It was joyions."Of course it was hard work, going to bed after midnight and getting up to see the Swiss soldier man digging trenches at 5 a.m. As the same writer remarks members of Parlia- ment were to be seen "standing asleep on the edge of giddy gorges "as a result of this strenuous life. To resume, we drove out one morning,along the road which twists and turns up the slopes of the Eigenthal. Here we saw one company of recruits skirmishing against another. Nothing very special except—and it is a big except—that these lads of taventy were carrying a weight of nearly 701bs. including rifle and ammunition. For the Swiss soldier is self contained. He carries on his back that which makes him independent of baggage waggons, and at night, no matter how rough the storm, he lies safe and snug under the shelter teut which be has helped to carry. At mid-day the cease fire sounded and preparation for lunch ensued. Some went off to get water; others cut down brush wood, others again became potato peelers, while those architecturally inclined made the most fascinating little hearths out of stones and mess tins. In a very short time the ration of meat and potatoes was transformed intoa stew which rejoiced the hearts not only of the recruits bat but of the whole Committee, the House of Lords and the House of Commons sitting down in perfect harmony. These recruits enjoyed their training. They were bright, cheery and vigorous. To them it was a holiday. It would be similarly a grand holiday for our working population if they went to a school of recruits out in the country for a few months. This surely is quite clear. When his training is finished the recruit is counted a soldier. He is enrolled in his local regiment and nextyear spends 18 days on manceuvre, and goes out training every subsequent two years up the age of 32. Men up to this age constitute the elite which numbered I n 1906. 137,000 men. From 32 up to 44, they are transferred to the reserve or Landwchr and. are only called out once for a similar period of 18 days This of course means a certain dislocation of business. but with hardly an exception the employers of labour are enthusiastic over the army, and submit cheerfully to the temporary inconvenience of having 10 per cent. of their men away for a fortnight. In fact what struck us all, labour members included, was the wonderful spirit which animated the people from the highest to

div.head: Passive Resistance at Frodsham.
div.p: Passive Resistance at Frodsham.

Sir,—Until I read Press accounts of police court proceedings on September ISth, I was quite entirely unaware of the significance v4hich was supposed to attach to my movements when leaving the court. I did not hear the reported outcry from the Bench nor the gay and festive—if somewhat stale—implication of the Clerk of the Court. Unlike the Quaker leader who put his hat on in church in protest against false doctrine, I resumed the head-covering without consciousness of any symbolic significance in the act (just before passing through the door-way which is my customary method of protection from chill). Your reporter in his admir- ably accurate notes, somewhat fails to do justice to the huh-hub of opposition to my speaking the half-dozen, sentences in "showing cause," as called to do by the summons. After a long tedious hour, concerning the angle of a lamp-bracket on a motor-car, the time of the court suddenly became abnormally precious. Yet mine was also a question of light and of public interest. To deny me these minutes in which to state the position appeared to be straining the technical forms of officialism. The time-pressure plea fails to do justice either to the intelligence of the public (to which we appeal) or to the sagacity of the Bench. When courtesy and consideration—as shown in other courts (whose responsibilities take wider range) are locally ousted out, the public intelligence will know why, and that episode is in keeping. My place was in the passage, a few paces from the door—and as I passed. out, with no thought of disrespect. I must have crowned myself a moment too soon, and for that moment exposed myself to the alert eye of the Bench. " Take that hat off !" Ala,ck and well-a-day ! Sir, had the injurious, strident, rebuking demand reached my ears I should have obeyed with sincere and genuine apologetic gesture, even at the door, and I should have gone forth, hat in hand. But, for the life of me, in such case, I could not have refrained from thinking of that terror of small children, Mr. Bumble- the-Beadle. J. SLACK, United Methodist Church, Frodsham.

div.head: COLLARS FOR FOXHOUNDS.
div.p: COLLARS FOR FOXHOUNDS.
Sir Gilbert Greenell's Action

At the Bourne (Lincolnshire) Police Court, on Thurs- day, a case of considerable interest,to followers of the Duke of Rutland's Hounds was heard. Arthur E. Bradley, of Rinpingale, was summoned for having a foxhound in his possession without a collar with the owner's name. Mr. Theodore Norton, acting upon instructions of Sir Gilbert Greenall, the Master, defended, and submitted that the foxhound puppy came within the expression "pack of hounds" which were exempted from the regulations. Ben Capel, the huntsman, declared that the effect of the Bench convicting would be the ruination of the breeding of foxhounds, and also would make it a difficult matter to hunt. The Bench dismissed the snmmons.

div.head: MAYORALTY.
div.p: THE MAYORALTY.
Deputation Waits on Alderman Smethurst.

We understand that the deputation appointed by the Town Council on Monday, as reported on pago 13, waited upon Alderman Smethurst yesterday and requested that he would accept the Mayoralty for another year. Testimony was borne to his Worship's valuable services as chief magistrate, and the strong hope was expressed that he would see his way to again occupy the position. Alderman Smethurst did not give a definite reply, but promised that the matter should receive his careful consideration. His decision will, it is expected, be made known at the meeting of the Council on Tuesday evening next.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

A LOCAL INVENTION AT ALTR INC HAM Snow.— Much interest was evinced at Altrincham Agricultural Show in the exhibit of Messrs. Ward and Hight in of Fearnhead, of a new potatoes digger which they have Invented and patented. Several interesting trials of the machine have been made of late in the district and photographs taken while it has been at work and these photographs were shown and attracted considerable attention. The machine looks like effecting a con- siderable saving of hand labour and should be a great boon to farmers. A certificate of merit for excellence of exhibit was accorded by the judges.

Oddferlows' Bowling Main. A very successful function was the distribution of prizes to winners of the fifth bowling handicap in connection with the Prince of Wales Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows which took place at the Pelican Hotel ox Thursday evening. There was adarge attendance. Bro. T. P. Bradshaw, P.P.G.M. presided, and was supported by Bros. W. Holbrook, P.G.M. (Warrington District), Lot Brooks D.G.M., F. Webster, CS., T. Wadsworth, P.G., J. Massey, P.P.G.M., W. Penningtou P.G., (National Order of Oddfellows) and G. F. Freeman P.G. (secretary of the bowling committee). The Chairman expressed his gratification at the posi- tion which the lodge held at present. They had a capital of .4:3,400, well invested, and they had a membership of 480, which was steadily increasing. He hoped the members would do all in their power to maintain the position of the lodge. (Applause.)—Bro. Holbrook congratulated the winners on their success. —The following is the prize list: 1, J. Howard, cup and medal; 2 D. Bromley, 3 A. Cooper, 4 J. P. Whittaker, 5 H. Cook, 6 T. P. Throssell, 7 R. H. Halford, sen., 8 G. F. Freeman, 9 H. Maddock, 10 F. Wisedale, 11 H. Glover, 12 H. Haslarn, 13 J. Ken- wright, 14 W. Roughley, and 15 D. Ferguson. A smoking concert was held and songs were rendered by the following :—Bros. J. Willett, R. Ray, Lot Brooks, Price, A. Boyle, P. Lee, and P. Sutton. Bro. Pemberton accompanied. Bro. Wadsworth proposed a vote of thanks to the officers in attendance and hoped that they would continue to give the lodge their hearty support and co-operation. Bro. Boyle seconded and the motion was carried unanimously. A vote of thanks was accorded to the artistes.

div.head: LIBERALS AT BELLE VllE.
div.p: LIBERALS AT BELLE VllE.
SUCCESSFUL PICNIC, --- Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., on the Governmeint's Record.

The Liberal picnic to Belle Vue on Saturday was a splendid success. The arrangements were perfect, the weather was genial, and the 1,500 members of the various progressive organizations and friends who made the journey to the famous pleasure resort agreed that the outing was one of the most enjoyable they had experienced. To transport the excursionists to Belle Vile three special trains were required, and these left Central Station at intervals from one to two o'clock. The Cheshire Lines Committee placed admirable facilities at the disposal of the huge party, and the trains were all got away in good time under the super- vision of Mr. Darbyshire the stationmaster. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P , and Miss Crosfield travelled by the first train and received a hearty welcome from the Liberal workers. It was noticed with pleasure that the Borough Member had evidently benefited from his sojourn in Switzerland and was looking very well. Mr. and Miss Crosfield both took a great interest in the excursion and it was no doubt gratifying to them that everything passed off without a , hitch. On arrival at Belle Vue, the visitors made their way to the Gardens to the martial strains of Messrs. Crosfield's band, which was in great form and played in highly creditable style. Belle Vue is a household word in this part of the country and the Warringtonians were soon busy sampling its mani- fold attractions. Dancing afforded delight to many, and others indulged in trips on the lake and the excitements of the" ocean wave" and the helter-skelter light-house. The remarkably fine collection of animals, of course, came in for a great deal of atten- tion and all afternoon groups of visitors were to be seen admiring the rare specimens. Others found pleasure in strolling about the trimly-kept gardens. At five o'clock an excellent tea was served in the large hall. Messrs. Jennison are experts at catering for large numbers, and the wants of the party could not have been more expeditiously attended to. At the cross table were seated many prominent Liberals. Alderman Tinnion presided and was sup- ported by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., and Miss Oros- field ; Councillors Wilkinson and Clegg, Mr. S. Wright, Mr. Joseph Howes, Mrs. and Miss Howes, Mr. Joseph Howes, jun., Mr. and Mrs. W. Furness, Mr. J. T. Locker /hon. secretary of the association) and Mrs. Locker, Mrs. Osborne, Mrs. Felix Maginn, Mr. W. Bibby, Mr. George Walker, Mr. Joseph-tVilkinson,Mr. Peter Peacock, Mr. and Mrs. T. Pemberton, Mr. F. Plimpton, Mr. T. Critchley, Mr. and Mrs. Jalues Critchley, Mr. H. Gorst, Mr. and Mrs. O'Brien, Mr. T. Barnes, Mr. J. Willett, and Mr. J. Tilwell. During tea Messrs. Oros-field's band played the " Poet and Peasant "overture and other choice selections in a manner which called forth warm applause. The Borough Member, who had an extremely cordial reception, afterwards delivered an interesting address on the work of the Government, which will be found fully reported below. In the evening there was more dancin, and the cene as viewed from the grand stand was full of animation. Several excursions from other parts had made Belle Vue their destination and the grounds were thronged. To see many hundreds of people " trioping the light fantastic toe " was a striking spectacle not readily to be forgotten. The great event for which most of the Warringtonians were waiting, however, was the firework display which began at 8.45. It was one of wonderful brilliance, for there were showers of rockets and many beautiful devices in flame. The climax was a thrilling representation of the "Battle of Blenheim" where Marlborough gained his" famous victory." A magnificent set piece had been painted and at a given signal this was dazzlingly illuminated and hostilities commenced. A great array of "troops" appeared and engaged in fierce combat to the accompaniment of the incessant booming of cannon and the explosion of shells. It was a grand spectacle and the concluding device which beautifully represented the "Entente Cordiale" was warmly cheerell. The first train left Belle Vue shortly before ten o'clock and the others followed at 10 and 10.15, Warrington being safely reached after an eminently successful outing. Great praise is due to the follow- ing committee which had the arrangements in hand : Mrs. Osborne and Mrs. F. Magian, and Messrs. T. Pemberton, W. Furness, P. Peacock, J. Morton, J. T. Locker, and J. Howes, jun. Special mention should be made of the services of Mr. Howes and Mr. HoTes, jun., who worked indefatigably to ensure that all should pass off well.
THE SPEECH-MAKING. MR. A. H. CROSFIELD AND THE GOVERNMENT'S RECORD.

After tea there was a little speech-making.—Alderman Tinnion, who presided, said he was pleased and proud to see such a vast assembly of the Liberal rank and tile, and he was particularly glad that the ladies were present in such large numbers. He was sure he vas echoing the sentiments of all present when be snid they were proud to have the presence of their Member, Mr. Arthur Crosfield—(applause)—and their pleasure was enhanced by the fact that his noble sister, Miss Truda Crostield, was also with them. (Applause.) Miss Crosfield set a splendid example to all who desired to further the progressive cause in Warrington, by her charming presence at their meetings and by helping in every pos- sible way to advance the work of the party and the interests of the greatest number of the working classes of Warrington. (Applause.) He had pleasure in calling upon the Member to address them. Mr. A. H. Croslield M.P., who was received with cheers, said he felt, like his friend Alderman Tinnion, a great deal of honest and sincere pleasure in having the

privilege of addressing ;that great gathering, of their fellow townspeople and also a great deal of pride to think that the Liberal party of Warrington mustered that day in that splendid and representative meeting. (Applause.) The Chairman had given him a timely hint that they did not want a very long speech on an occasion like that and he was reminded of what he heard said after a banquet the other day by a man who wanted to address his audience rather briefly and who remarked that he understood that the best speech that ever was made was delivered by Daniel in the den of lions when he said : "Thank heaven there wil be no after-dinner speeches at this banquet." (Loud laughter.) He (Mr. Crosfleld) was afraid he could not make his speech quite as short as Daniel's on that historic occasion, but he would not trespass on their time by attempting to discuss political questions in detail. It would not be fair when they had so many attractions outside much greater than any poor political effort he could make. At the same time he would ask them to bear with him while he briefly enumerated some of

THE LEGISLA.TIVE ACHIETENIENTS of the'Government and tried to indicate the work of the future, because he could assure them that they who were closely in touch with the work of the party felt— and they hoped at the meetings which would be held between now and Christmas to prove—that both in regard to legislation and administration they had an honest and sincere Government which, he ventured to think, compared with all other Governments had already broken the record in respect of good work. (Applause.) He would mention several of the chief items in the pro- gramme which so far had bcen carried out and to which they hoped to add equally good and useful items of work in the period that yet remained to this Parlia- ment. Perhaps it would not be a bad thing to mention some of the work that had been done on behalf of the children in the first instance because, after all, in build- ing up a great and noble State they could not forget that it was well to lay the foundations early on in life and to begin with the children, and so the Government had passed an Act, the object of which was to

CARR FOR DEFECTIVE CHILDREN. and they had taken care that, with proper precautions, children who needed it should be fed when they went to school. (Hear, hear.) They had arranged for vacation schools for children who were neglected in holiday time and they had also provided for medical inspection of children in schools, which he considered was a matter of great importance. They had passed an Act—and he would draw the ladies' attention especially to this—which forbade the employment of women at night in mines and factories, and another measure,which it had bden estimated would affect 200,000 women in England, safeguarded their work in laundries and such establishments. Another important Act was the

MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, the object of which was to see that our sailors had sufficient air space in their vessels, that they got decent food, and that there were cooks on board shin properly qualified to do their cooking. A very homely measure if they liked—and so were some of the others, but the Government ventured to think that each of those Acts was calculated to level up the condition of labour amongst sections of our people who had been less able by. their own organizations to kelp themselves. AU representatives of trade unions pre..ent knew the immense advantage of that collective bargaining which he had always felt from the bottom of his heart to be fair as between employers and employed. They all knew hew that principle had been strengthened by

TRADIIS DISPUTES BILL which had been passed—(applause) —and in spite of the gloomy vaticinations which he read of,he ventured to tell kis friend Mr. David Garnett that that Act and collec- tive bargaining did not make for industrial warfare but, in the long run, for industrial peace. (Applause.) He was sure that everybody in that gathering knew of the great extension of the Workmen's Compensation Act— an extension affecting no less than six millions of the people of this country, now that the Government had included in the operation of that Act, domestic servants, seamen, postmen, clerks and shop assistants. He could not conclude his brief survey without alluding to two great Acts connected with

THE I,AD of this country. They passdd in 1905 the Land Tenure , Act which was generally regarded in the House of Commons as the farmers' charter. (Applause.) It secured compensation for improvements on holdings ; gave compensation for damage done by game; secured freedom for cropping and disposal of produce: and gave compansation for unreasonable disturb- ance. He submitted that that was not any uproot- ing of individualism. It was not improper inter- ference with the rights of private property, but it helped to make individualism and the rights of private ownership fairer to all concerned. The next great Act was the Small Holdings Act for England, by which compulsory powers for pnichasing land were given to County and Borough Councils, and those authorities were also empowered to borrow money and repay it in sixty years in order to make the Act effec- tive. He noticed the other day that Mr. Pierpoint referred to the question of population in foreign countries and in our own land. In the first place might he say that the Government regarded not only the ques- tion of population, but also how our population in England was to be distributed ? He would suggest to Mr. Pierpoint this consideration—that it was by Mr. Harcourt's Land Bill that they would best be able to get the labourer back to the soil. (Applause.) Between the years 1881 and 1907—say in the last genera- tion—roughly speaking. our English labourers on the soil had diminished from a million to 700,000. That drop of 300,000 out of a million was a serious matter for the country and for the national physique, and it was by giving the small holder a chance of a fair rettsrn on his labour and enterprise, a reason- able amount of independence and some pride and interest in life in his own local centre, that they would best stop too great a drain from the country districts to the towns. By that one improvement and in many other ways they would help to maintain and improve the physique of the manhood of the nation. (Applause). He could enumerate many items of legislation, and he could assure his hearers that if they would be kind enough to come to the meetings they were arranging in Warrington for the autumn, they would be pleased to tell them what the Government had done and what they wanted to do. They would be perfectly frank, because they really felt proud of their record and verx hopeful of what they were yet going to achieve. He would, however, complete his list on the present occa- sion by referring to the EVIC FED TENANTS' BILL for Ireland. He knew that the object of Mr. Birrell— one of the most single-minded, honest and earnest men they ever had in English politics—(applause)—was to
For Children's Hacking Cough at night, Woods' Great Peppermint Cure. 1/11, 219.

try and get rid of the last remains of bad feeling and to stop the last drop of bad blood circulating in the country districts of Ireland, and it was a thousand pities that the House of Lords did not allow the Bill to go through as he submitted it. There would still be unfortunate people in Ireland who should have been put back on their holdings but who would be left by the roadside. It created bad blood, it was bad policy. and it had not been just. While he wished to see the landlord receive exact compensation—market value— wherever compulsory purchase was necessary in Ireland to carry out the Government policy, he thought it was too bad that they should have to pay 22 per cent above the market value, and it was a shame that they should have to draw the line at 2,000 when there might be 5,000 or 6,000 people to be re-instated. Finally it was too bad to so al#er the Bill as to prevent the Government dealing with the estate of Lord Clanricard who had been more responsible for bad feeling in his quarter of the country than perhaps all the other land- lords in that neighbourhood put together. (Applause.) All that the Government had done in the way of legislation was not everything. Administration counted for a very great deal and at this juncture- he thought everyone would call it significattt that in the Postal Service and in the Admirality the Government authorities had

RECOGNIZED THE ACCREDITED LEADERS who with their expert knowledge represented the workers. (Hear, hear.) If they had recognized Associations in the Post Office and in the Admirality then he respectfully asked why not on the railways ? (Applause.) Mr. Crosfibld then thanked the gathering for listening to that brief recital which he trusted he might have the privilege of enlarging upon on other occasions this autumn. He know that even what they had done made many good but timid people say 'O, you dreadful people. You are working not for a fall. You are working for revolu- tion." (Laughter.) They never made a bigger mistake. To the work they had clone the Government hoped to add better provision still for the children and the aged, and better chances of getting the full value out of agricultural development in England, and when they had done it all, believe him it was not revolution they were seeking, for the result of those efforts would be a wider spread of contentment and of the best kind of happiness and therefore,he submitted a nobler future for our nation and greater stability in this dear old England of ours and throughost the Empire too.( Loud applause.) At the call of Alderman Tinnion, the assembly then gave three hearty cheers for the Member and Miss Crosfleld.

Presentation to Mr. W. Taylor. Thursday last was the occasion of a pleasing core— moray at the offices of the Wesleyan and General Assurance S .ciety, Cairo-street, when Mr. William Taylor, the genial superintendent of the district, -0"59' made the recipient of a presentation by the agents and , staff. The presentation took the form of a beautiful)/ illaininated address and a handsome smoker's cabinet. The address testified to the sterling manly qualitie9. the abilities and the kindly, generous nature of the recipient, regret at his departure, but felicitations upon his attaining greater honours. The cordiality and g-.)odwill which animated one and all present the meeting when the interesting event took place, plainly evinced that these sentiments sprang not frorn the lips. but from the heart. Mr. Taylor, who has. laboured most successfully in this town for his Society. upwards of eighteen years, is leaving Warrington to. take ehargo of the important district of Gateshead and carries with him the good wishes of all who take. pride in an o:d Warringtonian's success.

Warrington Cycling Club. On Saturday last the season was brought to a close' when a bowling main was held at Sankey. The bowl- ing green at the Sankey Chapel House was reserved for the use of the men-berg, and some good bovvling and exciting games were witnessed. The winners Of the prizes were :-1, G. F. Freeman; 2, J. Bellian ; 3, G. H. Smith; 4, W. Unsworth. An excellent tes was provided by Mr. Ijnsworth, and about 30 members' were then present.—After tea an interesting presenta- tion was made tn Mr. George Bowman, in commemora— tion of his recent marriage.—The captain made the ' presentation, which took the form of a dressing-room clock and ornaments, of original and elaborate design, and referred to the splendid services rendered by Mr. Bowman to the club. Other members also gave expression io the esteem in which Mr. Bowman was held by his fellow members. Suit— able response was made by Ur. Bowman who thanked the members on behalf of his wife and himself for the handsome and valuable present and expressed her appreciation of the spirit which prompted the gift- Other presentations of prizes in connection with the various competitions were also made. A smokiflg. concert was then proceeded with ; songs, duets and quartettes were rendered by Messrs. F. Fieldhouse• J. B. Poole, S. Hassan, W. A. Clay and C. H. Houh and recitations by Miss G. B. Kendrick and A. ClaY• Mr. Pearce accompanied the singers on the piart°' Altogether the function was very enjoyable and one of the most successful held under the auspices o f to club.

Good News for Cheshire Workers. Mr. J. 11. Davies, of Manchester, president of the, Manchester United Football Club, and also connecte3 with local brewery companies, recently discovered new salt-producing area at Plumbley, near Nortb wich, on some land owned by him. An extensive examina" tion and boring has proved that the brine supply 03 the land is abundant, and the property has been sold by I.lr. Davies, probably for a very large sum, to the Ammonia Soda Company, composed of Mr. Arthur Chamberlain (brother to the Right Hon. Joseph . Chamberlain), Mr. A. Chamberlain, jun., Mr. Iva 3 Levinstein of Manchester, Mr. J. S. Nettlefold, 3fr' Cothing, and others. The Ammonia Soda Comnuni intend to erect a huge chemical works at Plumble-y an early date, and a large number of hands will 110 doubt be required.

COUNTY PALATINE OF CHESTER. I\TOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next IN GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY PALATINE OF CHESTER will be holden at the COURT HOUSE, KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the FOURTEENTH day of OCTOBER, 1907, at Eleven o'clock in tbe Fore- noon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The bearing of all Appeals arising within the Petty Sessional Divisions of Al trincham,Bucklow, Dukinfleld, Middlewich, Sandbacb, Congleton, Northwicb,Prestbury, and Stockport. forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from such Divisions, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Knutsford District must he in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the Opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 14th day of October next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE COURT will be Adjourned to the CASTLE OF CHESTER on WEDNESDAY, the SIXTEENTH day of OCTOBER,. 1907„at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Petty Sessional Divisions of Broxton, Chester Castle, Dares- bury, Eddisbury, Nantwich, Runcorn, Winsford, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-mentioned Divisions, will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on WEDNESDAY, the 16th day of October, 1907, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the County Palatine of Chester. Chester, 23rd September, 1907.
